Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), ethylene carbonate (EC), and methyl ethyl carbonate (EMC) were supplied by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co., Ltd. A baseline electrolyte was prepared by dissolving NaPF $_6$ (1 mol/L) into a mixed solvent of EC and EMC (weight ratio 3:7). To formulate a functional electrolyte, 1 wt% 2-Sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA) was added to the baseline system. The NFM cathode and hard carbon (HC) anode active materials were procured from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. and Kuraray Co., Ltd., respectively. The NFM cathode slurry consisted of 94.5 wt% NFM, 1.8 wt% PVDF, 1 wt% carbon nanotubes (CNT), 2.5 wt% Super P, and 0.2 wt% maleic acid dispersed in $N$ -methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and was cast onto aluminum foil. The HC anode was composed of 95 wt% HC,

citations.quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

citations.quote:
ABSTRACT
A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs. This work presents a practical strategy for development of all-climate carbonate electrolyte and it offers the straight approach to high-performance commercial pouch SIBs.

In summary, we have successfully synthesized a multifunctional SA electrolyte additive for pouch NFM/HC sodium-ion batteries, enabling stable electrochemical performance across a wide operating temperature range ( $-20$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ ). The multifunctional role of the SA-containing electrolyte can be attributed to a combination of synergistic effects, including the regulation of $Na^{+}$ solvation structure to accelerate interfacial reaction kinetics and enhance electrochemical stability at low temperatures, the scavenging residual water to preserve the structural stability of the cathode and suppress excessive gas evolution, thereby enhancing high-temperature performance, and the preferential redox decomposition of SA on the anode surface to form a high-quality interfacial film that protects the electrode and reduces interfacial resistance. Collectively, this work provides new insights into the rational design and optimization of electrolyte additives for practical all-climate pouch SIBs and other advanced energy storage systems.

citations.chunk_id: 0156_Cai 等 - 2025 - A hard-soft synergy strategy enables drastic temperature performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries o::sec2
citations.quote:
ABSTRACT
A “hard-soft synergy” strategy is firstly developed to design functional multi-component electrolytes and successfully achieve drastic temperature performance of $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) over a wide range from $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . Coupling “hard”-sodium difluorophosphate (NaDFP) with “soft”-tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphate (TMSP) or tris(trimethylsilyl) borate (TMSB) reasonably realizes an optimized solvation structure from “solvent dominated” to “anion collaborative” and synergistic-formed tough and multi-component interfacial films. Benefit to these, the cycling stability is considerably improved under the room and cold conditions, the capacity retention after 350 cycles increases from 0 % to 92 % and even stable cycling performance at 1 C (1 C = 900 mA) can be obtained at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ . Discharge capacity at $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ and the capacity retention after storage at $60\ ^{\circ}C$ are also greatly improved. Furthermore, the functional mechanisms of different electrolyte combinations under extreme temperature conditions are analyzed. It is demonstrated that the combination of NaDFP and TMSP is more suitable for high-temperature requirements due to its tougher cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI), reduced transition metal dissolution, and minimized cathode phase deviation. In contrast, the combination of NaDFP and TMSB is more suitable for low-temperature requirements, benefiting from the reduced desolvation energy and viscosity. In addition to the obtained functional electrolytes, this work also provides new insight for designing functional multi-component electrolytes of SIBs.

Similar to high-temperature performance of pouch cells, these "hard-soft synergy" functional electrolytes induce amazing low-temperature performance of NFM/HC SIBs. As shown in the Figs 4a, 4b and S5a, both pouch cells with the NB or NP electrolyte can improve the cycling performance compared to the cells with the baseline electrolyte, an excellent capacity retention of $95\%$ after 350 cycles and high stability can be obtained benefiting from the "hard-soft synergy". With the help of "hard-soft synergy", polarization and capacity fading are alleviated signally during the cycling.

citations.quote: Firstly, the electrolyte was injected into the pouch NNFM111/HC cells in an argon-filled glove box and then the cells were deposited at room temperature for 24 h. The cells were first charged at 0.1 C constant current for 390 min with a pressure of $3 \, kg cm^{-2}$ . After charging, the cells were put at $45^{\circ}$ C for 24 h with a pressure of $3 \, kg cm^{-2}$ . All cells were activated by charging and discharging at 0.1 C, 0.2 C, 0.5 C, and 1 C. The charge and discharge tests of the NNFM111/HC full cells were conducted using a battery test system (CT-3008 W, Neware, China) at a voltage range of 2.0-4.0 V. The cycle performance of NNFM111/HC full cells was measured at a constant temperature of $25^{\circ}$ C and $45^{\circ}$ C with a charge and discharge current of 1 C. The discharge curves of the NNFM111/HC full cells at $-20^{\circ}$ C were measured in a temperature controlled test chamber at the discharge rates of 0.5 C and 1 C. The ratio of the discharge capacity of the cell at $-20^{\circ}$ C to the last discharge capacity of the cell activated at room temperature was taken as the capacity retention rate of the cell at low temperature. The cells with 50% state of charge (SOC) discharged at a current rate of 2 C for 10 s at $-20^{\circ}$ C. The direct current resistance (DCR) was calculated on the basis of Ohm's law (R=U/I).

papers: 0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage

citations.chunk_id: 0074_Yang 等 - 2026 - Weak-solvation dilution for interphase preservation and extreme low-temperature sodium-ion storage::sec4::child0
citations.quote:
The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory. The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison.

citations.quote:
Electrolyte design
The strong electron-withdrawing ability of the F atom reduces the electronic density on the coordinated O atom, reducing the solvation power $[21]$ . Comparing fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) with EC, F-substitution reduces the donor number to dissolve salts but it does not bind to cations too tightly $[22,23]$ . However, weaker solvation comes with increased cluster size and viscosity. For example, the FEC/PC solvent system (brown)

presents a weaker solvation ability than EC/PC (red). The mobility of the cation cluster decreases as the cluster size and medium viscosity increase. For pure carbonates, interphasial kinetics and ionic transportation mitigation are always contradictory.

The low melting point (below $-90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and mild donor number (8.4) are distinctive properties of MDFA for low-temperature batteries [19] but the low dielectric constant (10.1) makes it hard to dissolve sufficient sodium ions for high ionic conductivity (Fig. S1a). Alternatively, utilizing these properties of MDFA as a diluting agent is reasonable for obtaining a weak-solvation electrolyte. Through this weak-solvation dilution strategy, a fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid low-concentration electrolyte, $0.25\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC/MDFA (1:1:2 in vol%) (0.25 FPM), is established by using MDFA to dilute $0.5\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in FEC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (0.5 FP). $1.0\mathrm{MNaClO_4}$ in EC/PC (1:1 in vol%) (1.0 EP) is used for comparison. In Scheme 1, the low concentration of $0.5\mathrm{M}$ sodium salt in 0.5 FP reduces viscosity and provides a higher degree of salt dissociation. Therefore, the ratio of strongly binding contact ion pairs (CIPs) decreases. As MDFA is introduced into 0.5 FP, when it replaces the large FEC and PC molecules in the solvation structure (blue), the mobility of the cation cluster increases as the size of the cation cluster reduces. CONCLUSION
In this work, the weak-solvation dilution strategy is successfully employed to establish a low-concentration fluorinated carboxylic ester/carbonate hybrid electrolyte, 0.25 FPM, which features a low melting point, low viscosity, wide ESW, low interphase dissolution and exceptional performance at low temperatures. This strategy simultaneously and jointly promotes bulk ionic transportation, desolvation and interphasial kinetics of carbonate-based electrolytes, enabling cells to function at low temperatures. The F-rich, thin but robust interphases generated by 0.25 FPM are protective and diffusion-friendly. The reduced inorganic salt dissolution rate of 0.25 FPM also guarantees the stabilization of interphases. Meanwhile, the low-temperature capacity retention of 0.25 FPM stands in the top tier among the reported electrolytes. At 25°C, prototype NFPP||HC with 0.25 FPM achieves a maximum power density of 2000 W kg $^{-1}$ (40 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ). Even at an extremely low temperature of -70°C, this SIB outputs an energy density of 60 Wh kg $^{-1}$ . With 0.25 FPM, the NNFMO||HC pouch cell maintains a high capacity retention of 83% and energy retention of 65% at -30°C. This strategy offers new insights into tuning ionic transportation and interphasial kinetics of electrolytes for extreme temperature applications.

With 0.25 FPM, HC delivers 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 mA g $^{-1}$ , with an ICE of 72%. For avoiding Na plating and high-rate purpose, the prototype full cell is thus designed to have excess HC. NFPP is used as the cathode to provide sufficient working ability at low temperatures, and this prototype full cell is denoted as NFPP||HC; the prototype cell has an initial discharge capacity of 87vmAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C (Fig. 5a).

NFPP||HC delivers 80, 72, 66, 60, 48 and $28\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ at 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0 and $10.0\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 5b). Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) show significant promise for their abundance and potential fast kinetics. However, ether-based electrolytes are limited by low anodic stability, and carbonate electrolytes typically suffer from reduced conductivity and sluggish desolvation at lower temperatures. Here, a weak-solvation dilution strategy that utilizes methyl difluoroacetate (MDFA) as a weakly solvated diluting agent to prepare an optimized carbonate/ester hybrid electrolyte is reported. MDFA reduces the bulk viscosity and takes part in the solvation structures to promote bulk ionic transportation and desolvation. Meanwhile, the reduced interaction between sodium and the solvent system limits salt dissolution to improve the interphase durability. The optimized electrolyte has an energy density of $60\mathrm{Whkg}^{-1}$ at $-70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a full cell using $\mathrm{Na_4Fe_3(PO_4)_2P_2O_7}$ (NFPP) and hard carbon (HC), which exceeds the current limitation of carbonate electrolytes.

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

ABSTRACT: Common battery electrolytes comprise organic carbonate solvents and fluorinated salts based on hexafluorophosphate (PF $_6^-$ ) anions. However, these electrolytes suffer from high flammability, limited operating temperature window, and high cost. To address those issues, we here propose a fluorine-free electrolyte based on sodium bis(oxalate)borate (NaBOB). Although lithium bis(oxalate)borate (LiBOB) has previously been investigated for lithium-ion batteries, NaBOB was considered too insoluble in organic solvents to be used in practice. Here, we show that NaBOB can be dissolved in mixtures of $N$ -methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and trimethyl phosphate (TMP) and in each sole solvent. NMP provides higher solubility of NaBOB with a concentration of almost 0.7 M, resulting in an ionic conductivity up to 8.83 mS cm $^{-1}$ at room temperature. The physical and electrochemical properties of electrolytes based on NaBOB salt dissolved in NMP and TMP solvents and their binary mixtures are here investigated. The results include the thermal behavior of the sole solvents and their mixtures, flammability tests, NaBOB solubility, and ionic conductivity measurements of the electrolyte mixtures.

However, those highly fluorinated electrolytes are subject to health concerns, especially the fluorinated carbon chains that have been shown to bio-accumulate in nature and the human body. $^{[9]}$

citations.quote: Furthermore, the application of phosphate-based electrolytes in high-temperature SIBs has rarely been reported. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a low-cost and environmentally friendly strategy for regulating the solvation structure, capable of constructing a stable EEI without relying on fluorine-containing components, thereby facilitating the practical application of phosphate-based electrolytes and ensuring the safe and stable operation of SIBs at elevated temperatures. In this work, we developed an intrinsically nonflammable and fluorine-free phosphate-based electrolyte for high-temperature SIBs by employing conventional carbonate cosolvents, ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC). The introduction of EMC modulates the ion-dipole interactions, leading to the formation of a multi-component synergistic solvation structure. This unique solvation structure facilitates the derivation of a stable EEI on both the cathode and anode, effectively suppressing continuous electrolyte decomposition and transition metal dissolution. Furthermore, the addition of EMC significantly reduces the viscosity and desolvation energy of the electrolyte system, thereby enhancing ion transport kinetics. As a result, the Prussian blue||hard carbon (PB||HC) full cell exhibits excellent temperature adaptability from 10 °C to 100 °C, and remains a high capacity of 79.6% after 400 cycles in 18,650 cylindrical cells.

citations.chunk_id: 0364_Zhou 等 - 2026 - A nonflammable carbonate-phosphate hybrid electrolyte enabling high-temperature sodium-ion full batt::sec2::child0
citations.quote: Developing high-safety electrolytes with wide-temperature applicability is a key challenge in advancing the practical application of sodium-ion batteries. In this work, we present a rational electrolyte design strategy that constructs an intrinsically nonflammable and fluorine-free electrolyte based on a carbonate-phosphate mixed solvent system, achieving a balance among cost-effectiveness, sustainability, safety, and temperature tolerance. The relatively weak coordination ability of ethyl methyl carbonate facilitates a favorable reorganization of solvation chemistry at conventional concentrations, promoting greater incorporation of anions and additives into the primary $Na^{+}$ solvation sheath. This leads to the preferential formation of a robust electrode-electrolyte interphase, effectively resolving the persistent issue of phosphate solvent decomposition at the anode interface. Moreover, the designed electrolyte features intrinsic nonflammability, low viscosity, high ionic conductivity, and rapid interfacial kinetics. As a result, the Prussian blue||hard carbon full cell demonstrates outstanding cycling stability over a temperature range from 10 °C to 100 °C. More importantly, both Ah-level pouch cells and 18,650 cylindrical cells exhibit superior electrochemical performance, strongly validating the considerable industrial potential of this electrolyte design strategy.

2.1. Electrolyte design
Although phosphate-based electrolytes possess intrinsic high safety, their practical application faces two major challenges (Fig. 1a): (i) Poor compatibility with electrode materials, which is attributed to the strong coordination ability of phosphate molecules that induces the phosphate-dominated solvation structure [19]. This leads to the unstable EEI with continuous electrolyte decomposition and severe capacity degradation, which aggravates at elevated temperatures. (ii) Inherently high viscosity, which limits ion transport and rate capability [26]. To address these issues, this work introduces a cosolvent with weak coordination ability and low viscosity, aiming to modulate the ion-dipole interactions within the phosphate ester-based electrolyte and optimize its physicochemical properties. The resulting multi-component synergistic solvation structure is expected to facilitate the formation of a stable EEI, thereby fundamentally improving electrolyte-electrode compatibility and enabling the practical application of phosphate ester-based electrolytes in high-safety SIBs. Meanwhile, $NaClO_{4}$ is selected due to its greater commercial maturity compared to high-cost fluorinated salts (such as NaFSI and NaTFSI), offering significant cost effectiveness for large-scale popularization. Although the strong oxidizing nature of $NaClO_{4}$ introduces certain safety concerns, pairing it with intrinsically non-flammable phosphate-based solvents and strictly implementing safety operation procedures can effectively mitigate potential safety risks.

citations.quote: To further evaluate the practical relevance of NTE electrolyte, PB|| HC full cells with high-mass loading electrodes are assembled (Fig. 4a). Full cells with NTE electrolyte significantly outperform their NT counterpart, with a higher capacity of 126.8 vs. $105.9\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , a superior initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) of $82.0\%$ vs. $69.5\%$ , and better capacity retention of $81.2\%$ vs. $76.0\%$ after 200 cycles (Fig. 4b and c). As shown in Figs. 4d and S12, the NTE electrolyte enables markedly enhanced rate performance. The full cell delivers a high capacity of $128.9\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ , substantially exceeding the $97.1\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ achieved with the NT electrolyte. This advantage is maintained at a high rate of $1.5\mathrm{C}$ , where the NTE-based cell retains $69.2\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , in contrast to only $42.5\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ for the NT-based cell. When systematically compared in Fig. 4e, the NTE system exhibits significantly higher capacity retention across all tested current rates. The smaller polarization observed across various rates can be attributed to the formation of robust CEI/SEI layers and reduced desolvation energy in the NTE system. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is employed to evaluate the interfacial stability of PB||HC cells with different electrolytes in Figs. 4f, S13 and Table S8.

citations.chunk_id: 0364_Zhou 等 - 2026 - A nonflammable carbonate-phosphate hybrid electrolyte enabling high-temperature sodium-ion full batt::sec8
citations.quote:
2.5. High temperature tolerance and universality
The temperature tolerance of NTE electrolyte is further evaluated in sodium-ion full cell. As shown in Fig. 5a, PB||HC cells employing NTE maintain stable charge-discharge performance over a temperature range from 10 °C to 100 °C. Additionally, the cell with NTE achieves superior cycling performance at 55 °C, maintaining a high capacity of 100.1 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 100 cycles. This performance is significantly higher than that of the NT-based cell, which delivers only 72.4 mAh g $^{-1}$ under identical conditions (Figs. 5b and S17). Benefiting from the enhanced interfacial kinetics, the full cell with NTE electrolyte delivers excellent rate performance from 0.1 C to 1.5 C at 55 °C (Figs. 5c and S18). It maintains a reversible capacity of 96.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 1.5 C, corresponding to 79.7% capacity at 0.1 C. While rapid capacity degradation at high rates with large polarization is observed in full cell with NT electrolyte, indicating its inferior compatibility within the full-cell system (Fig. 5d). In addition, the self-discharge test indicates that full cell with NTE electrolyte demonstrates superior ICE of 85.4% and reduced potential drop of 362.6 mV at 55 °C, compared to 74.2% and 398.4 mV with NT electrolyte (Fig. S19).

As presented in Fig. 5e, the cylindrical cell using NTE electrolyte demonstrates a reversible capacity of 743.8 mAh after 50 cycles at 55 °C, corresponding to the high capacity retention of 93.0%. Besides, NTE-based cylindrical cell also demonstrates superior rate capacity at 55 °C in Figs. 5f and S20. Furthermore, the NTE electrolyte maintains robust cyclability in cylindrical cells even at 80 °C, retaining 89.7% of its initial capacity after 50 cycles (Fig. S21). The universality of NTE electrolyte is further validated in full cells incorporating a layered oxide (NFM) cathode. The NTE-based cells consistently exhibit enhanced long-term cycling stability and rate performance at both 25 °C and 55 °C, as substantiated in Fig. 5g, h and S22-S26. These collective findings confirm the universal applicability and superior high-temperature stability of the designed NTE electrolyte.

citations.chunk_id: 0364_Zhou 等 - 2026 - A nonflammable carbonate-phosphate hybrid electrolyte enabling high-temperature sodium-ion full batt::sec2::child0
citations.quote: Developing high-safety electrolytes with wide-temperature applicability is a key challenge in advancing the practical application of sodium-ion batteries. In this work, we present a rational electrolyte design strategy that constructs an intrinsically nonflammable and fluorine-free electrolyte based on a carbonate-phosphate mixed solvent system, achieving a balance among cost-effectiveness, sustainability, safety, and temperature tolerance. The relatively weak coordination ability of ethyl methyl carbonate facilitates a favorable reorganization of solvation chemistry at conventional concentrations, promoting greater incorporation of anions and additives into the primary $Na^{+}$ solvation sheath. This leads to the preferential formation of a robust electrode-electrolyte interphase, effectively resolving the persistent issue of phosphate solvent decomposition at the anode interface. Moreover, the designed electrolyte features intrinsic nonflammability, low viscosity, high ionic conductivity, and rapid interfacial kinetics. As a result, the Prussian blue||hard carbon full cell demonstrates outstanding cycling stability over a temperature range from 10 °C to 100 °C. More importantly, both Ah-level pouch cells and 18,650 cylindrical cells exhibit superior electrochemical performance, strongly validating the considerable industrial potential of this electrolyte design strategy.

By introducing weakly coordinating EMC into a phosphate-based system, greater incorporation of anions and additives into the inner $Na^{+}$ solvation sheath is constructed. This process facilitates the formation of robust and stable EEI on both electrodes, effectively suppressing continuous electrolyte decomposition and transition metal dissolution. The optimized electrolyte simultaneously achieves low viscosity, high ionic conductivity, and rapid interfacial kinetics. As a result, the PB||HC full cells demonstrate exceptional cycling stability over a temperature range from 10 °C to 100 °C. More importantly, the excellent performance is successfully validated in Ah-level pouch cells and 18,650 cylindrical cells, confirming its practical viability.

citations.quote: Furthermore, the application of phosphate-based electrolytes in high-temperature SIBs has rarely been reported. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a low-cost and environmentally friendly strategy for regulating the solvation structure, capable of constructing a stable EEI without relying on fluorine-containing components, thereby facilitating the practical application of phosphate-based electrolytes and ensuring the safe and stable operation of SIBs at elevated temperatures. In this work, we developed an intrinsically nonflammable and fluorine-free phosphate-based electrolyte for high-temperature SIBs by employing conventional carbonate cosolvents, ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC). The introduction of EMC modulates the ion-dipole interactions, leading to the formation of a multi-component synergistic solvation structure. This unique solvation structure facilitates the derivation of a stable EEI on both the cathode and anode, effectively suppressing continuous electrolyte decomposition and transition metal dissolution. Furthermore, the addition of EMC significantly reduces the viscosity and desolvation energy of the electrolyte system, thereby enhancing ion transport kinetics. As a result, the Prussian blue||hard carbon (PB||HC) full cell exhibits excellent temperature adaptability from 10 °C to 100 °C, and remains a high capacity of 79.6% after 400 cycles in 18,650 cylindrical cells.

The electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 0.8 M NaPF $_6$ in a mixture of EC: EMC = 3:7, and this electrolyte was assigned as baseline electrolyte. NFM active material, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotube (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and Maleic acid were dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) with a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate. The HC active material, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and conductive carbon black (Super P) with a mass ratio of 95:1.5:2:1.5 were mixed and dispersed in water, and then the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate. The areal loading of the anode and cathode was 16 g m $^{-2}$ and 33 g m $^{-2}$ , respectively.

citations.chunk_id: 0156_Cai 等 - 2025 - A hard-soft synergy strategy enables drastic temperature performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries o::sec2
citations.quote:
ABSTRACT
A “hard-soft synergy” strategy is firstly developed to design functional multi-component electrolytes and successfully achieve drastic temperature performance of $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) over a wide range from $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . Coupling “hard”-sodium difluorophosphate (NaDFP) with “soft”-tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphate (TMSP) or tris(trimethylsilyl) borate (TMSB) reasonably realizes an optimized solvation structure from “solvent dominated” to “anion collaborative” and synergistic-formed tough and multi-component interfacial films. Benefit to these, the cycling stability is considerably improved under the room and cold conditions, the capacity retention after 350 cycles increases from 0 % to 92 % and even stable cycling performance at 1 C (1 C = 900 mA) can be obtained at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ . Discharge capacity at $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ and the capacity retention after storage at $60\ ^{\circ}C$ are also greatly improved. Furthermore, the functional mechanisms of different electrolyte combinations under extreme temperature conditions are analyzed. It is demonstrated that the combination of NaDFP and TMSP is more suitable for high-temperature requirements due to its tougher cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI), reduced transition metal dissolution, and minimized cathode phase deviation. In contrast, the combination of NaDFP and TMSB is more suitable for low-temperature requirements, benefiting from the reduced desolvation energy and viscosity. In addition to the obtained functional electrolytes, this work also provides new insight for designing functional multi-component electrolytes of SIBs.

As shown in Fig. 2f, at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the TD73 battery had a specific capacity of $99.1\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ and consistent cycling performance, with a retention rate of $88.3\%$ after 100 cycles. However, the full cell with TD01 performs poorly at low temperatures, with an initial specific capacity of only $87.5\mathrm{mAhg}^{-1}$ , and rapid capacity decay with increasing cycles. This clearly shows that the inclusion of THF improves the performance of ether-based electrolytes at low temperature. It improves the stability of both layered oxide cathodes and HC anodes, while the assembled full cells also exhibit excellent electrochemical performance. To examine the interfacial dynamics of the electrolyte at low temperature, we analyzed the half-cell impedance data following 50 cycles at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The results indicated that TD73 demonstrated lower interfacial resistance (53.8 $\Omega$ ), while TD01 recorded a value of $64.11\Omega$ (Fig. 3a). The results demonstrate that the incorporation of THF diminishes the interfacial barrier and enhances reaction kinetics at low temperature. Furthermore, we examined the impedance variations of the TD73 half-cell from $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The Arrhenius equation $(\frac{1}{R_{ct}} = Aexp\left(\frac{-E_a}{RT}\right))$ allows for the calculation of activation energy through the fitting of impedance at various temperature.

citations.quote:
4. Conclusions
In summary, a commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ /hard carbon is fabricated in this work. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, the electrolyte additive adiponitrile (ADN) is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time, and the effects of the ADN on the performance improvement of the cathode material $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ are investigated for the first time. The results show that ADN can promote the formation of highly conductive and stable SEI film on the cathode material surface, and effectively improve the high-low-temperature performance and cycling stability of $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ as the cathode electrode material of sodium-ion batteries. In particular, the battery with 3% ADN shows the most obvious improvement, its discharge capacity increases by 10.5%, 8%, and 13% at the operating temperature of 45, -10, and -20 °C, respectively. For the cycling stability, the capacity retention rate of the battery without adding ADN drops rapidly to 75% after 40 cycles, while the capacity retention rate of the battery with 3% ADN can still reach 78% after 220 cycles. Adding ADN as electrolyte additive effectively improves the electrochemical performance of sodium ion batteries. That is because the formation of compact, stable, and effective SEI film on the surface of the cathode material after adding ADN as electrolyte additive. This work offers an insightful guidance for the practical application of high-performance cathode materials in sodium-ion batteries.

citations.chunk_id: 0156_Cai 等 - 2025 - A hard-soft synergy strategy enables drastic temperature performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries o::sec2
citations.quote:
ABSTRACT
A “hard-soft synergy” strategy is firstly developed to design functional multi-component electrolytes and successfully achieve drastic temperature performance of $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) over a wide range from $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . Coupling “hard”-sodium difluorophosphate (NaDFP) with “soft”-tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphate (TMSP) or tris(trimethylsilyl) borate (TMSB) reasonably realizes an optimized solvation structure from “solvent dominated” to “anion collaborative” and synergistic-formed tough and multi-component interfacial films. Benefit to these, the cycling stability is considerably improved under the room and cold conditions, the capacity retention after 350 cycles increases from 0 % to 92 % and even stable cycling performance at 1 C (1 C = 900 mA) can be obtained at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ . Discharge capacity at $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ and the capacity retention after storage at $60\ ^{\circ}C$ are also greatly improved. Furthermore, the functional mechanisms of different electrolyte combinations under extreme temperature conditions are analyzed. It is demonstrated that the combination of NaDFP and TMSP is more suitable for high-temperature requirements due to its tougher cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI), reduced transition metal dissolution, and minimized cathode phase deviation. In contrast, the combination of NaDFP and TMSB is more suitable for low-temperature requirements, benefiting from the reduced desolvation energy and viscosity. In addition to the obtained functional electrolytes, this work also provides new insight for designing functional multi-component electrolytes of SIBs.

The baseline electrolyte was prepared by dissolving $NaPF_{6}$ in a mixture of EC: EMC=3:7 to form a concentration of 0.8 mol $L^{-1}$ . Then, NaDFP was added into the baseline electrolyte to prepare the NaDFP electrolyte, and NaDFP and

TMSB or TMSP were respectively added into the baseline electrolyte and assigned as NB or NP electrolyte. All electrolytes were prepared in a dry argon filled glove box with both moisture and oxygen concentrations below 0.1 ppm. NFM was purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co, Ltd, HC was purchased from Kuraray Co Ltd. The pouch test cells with NFM cathode (120 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C), HC anode (290 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.05 C), and Celgard 2700 separator were assembled using the conventional assembly method. Therein, NFM active material, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotube (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and Maleic acid (the reason of addition maleic acid was shown in Table 1) were dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) with a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate to prepare the NFM cathode. The HC active material, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and conductive carbon black (Super P) with a mass ratio of 95:1.5:2:1.5 were mixed and dispersed in water, and then the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate to prepare the HC anode. The areal loading of the anode and cathode were 16.0 g m $^{-2}$ and 33.0 g m $^{-2}$ , respectively. The semi-finished pouch cells were dried under vacuum at 80 °C for 72 h before being moved into a glove box for injecting electrolyte. The size of prepared pouch cells was 52 mm × 5 mm × 100 mm.

citations.quote: In practical applications, the performance of SIBs under the low-temperature conditions has attracted more attention. Similarly, based on the actual use of SIBs, the impact of different electrolytes on the low-temperature performance of SIBs was also characterized by measuring the cycle performance and rate performance at $-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , as well as the rate and discharge performance at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Similar to high-temperature performance of pouch cells, these "hard-soft synergy" functional electrolytes induce amazing low-temperature performance of NFM/HC SIBs. As shown in the Figs 4a, 4b and S5a, both pouch cells with the NB or NP electrolyte can improve the cycling performance compared to the cells with the baseline electrolyte, an excellent capacity retention of $95\%$ after 350 cycles and high stability can be obtained benefiting from the "hard-soft synergy". Notably, though the capacity of the cells with NP or NB electrolyte both over $850\mathrm{mAh}$ (NB-859 mAh vs. NP-850 mAh) after 300 cycles, the NP group shows more fluctuant coulombic efficiency than the NB group, as shown in Fig. 4b. Additionally, the charge/discharge curves of the cells with NP, NB, and baseline electrolytes are shown in Fig. 4c. With the help of "hard-soft synergy", polarization and capacity fading are alleviated signally during the cycling.

citations.quote: With the help of "hard-soft synergy", polarization and capacity fading are alleviated signally during the cycling. Besides, rate performance of pouch cells is also improved by the synergistic effect of NP or NB electrolyte even at $-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1\mathrm{C}$ , as shown in Fig. 4d and S5b. Furthermore, to evaluate dual additive potential at tougher low-temperatures, $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ discharge tests are necessary. Fig. 4e shows the capacity retention of pouch cells at different discharge currents, revealing the cells all can exhibit good electrochemical performance under the tested temperature conditions. Even at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1\mathrm{C}$ , the discharge capacity of pouch cells with NP and NB electrolytes still achieves $729\mathrm{mAh}$ and $697\mathrm{mAh}$ , respectively. These results confirm that this co-additive addition strategy improves extremely low temperature performance of NFM/HC pouch cells. Summarily, compared to single additive or baseline electrolyte, NFM/HC pouch cells with multi-component functional electrolyte possess much better performance. Therein, the cells containing NP electrolyte have better room and high-temperature performance, and the cells containing NB electrolyte are more suitable for low-temperature application.

4. Conclusions
In summary, a commercially feasible sodium-ion pouch cell with $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ /hard carbon is fabricated in this work. According to the calculation of the frontier molecular orbital energy, the electrolyte additive adiponitrile (ADN) is selected as the electrolyte additive to improve the performance of sodium-ion battery for the first time, and the effects of the ADN on the performance improvement of the cathode material $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ are investigated for the first time. The results show that ADN can promote the formation of highly conductive and stable SEI film on the cathode material surface, and effectively improve the high-low-temperature performance and cycling stability of $Na_{0.76}Ni_{0.3}Fe_{0.4}Mn_{0.3}O_{2}$ as the cathode electrode material of sodium-ion batteries. In particular, the battery with 3% ADN shows the most obvious improvement, its discharge capacity increases by 10.5%, 8%, and 13% at the operating temperature of 45, -10, and -20 °C, respectively. For the cycling stability, the capacity retention rate of the battery without adding ADN drops rapidly to 75% after 40 cycles, while the capacity retention rate of the battery with 3% ADN can still reach 78% after 220 cycles. Adding ADN as electrolyte additive effectively improves the electrochemical performance of sodium ion batteries. That is because the formation of compact, stable, and effective SEI film on the surface of the cathode material after adding ADN as electrolyte additive. This work offers an insightful guidance for the practical application of high-performance cathode materials in sodium-ion batteries.

citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

citations.quote: In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

citations.quote: Glyme-based solvents generally offer a suite of desirable properties, including broad electrochemical stability, high ionic conductivity, and compatibility with electrode materials, making them promising candidates for SIB electrolytes [9,10]. Additionally, reducing the coordination strength of the solvent with $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ can accelerate the de-solvation process and enhance compatibility with HC anodes [11]. Modifying the solvent molecule structure appears promising for adjusting the interaction between the solvent and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ [12]. Consequently, we have extended the alkyl chain length of the DME molecule to obtain Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme, as shown in Fig. 1a-d, to investigate the impact of chain length on the electrochemical performance of HC. Electrostatic potential (ESP) diagrams demonstrate a strong interaction between $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and the oxygen atoms of glyme-based solvents, attributed to the localized negative charge on the oxygen atoms (indicated by the blue areas in the calculated ESP diagrams) [13]. For simplicity, the electrolytes (1.0 M) with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ dissolved in DME, Diglyme, Triglyme, and Tetraglyme are denoted as G1, G2, G3, and G4, respectively. The freezing points of these solvents, DME at $-58^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Diglyme at $-68^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Triglyme at $-45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and Tetraglyme at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , indicate their suitability for low-temperature applications [14,15].

Moreover, the ionic diffusion coefficients also vary across the four electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2i, the simulated self-diffusion coefficient of Na $^{+}$ in G1 (1.251×10 $^{-5}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ) is higher than those in G2 (4.829×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), G3 (2.210×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), and G4 (1.525×10 $^{-6}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ ), which aligns with the conductivity measurements shown in Fig. S7. In summary, glyme-based electrolytes with shorter chain lengths facilitate rapid de-solvation and efficient ionic diffusion (Fig. 2j), thus enhancing interfacial kinetics and promoting the formation of an anion-derived SEI, thereby contributing to improved electrochemical performance of the target electrode [7,25]. The above MD simulations, complemented by characterizations, have shed light on the nuanced interplay between sodium ion and solvents, and this interplay consequently affects the coordination structures in electrolytes. Predominantly, these coordination structures can be segmented into three distinct categories based on the proximity of cations to an anion: solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIP) with no cations in the immediate solvation shell, contact ion pairs (CIP) involving a single cation, and aggregates (AGG) where the anion associates with multiple cations [6].

citations.quote: Fig. 3c-f present high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of HC electrodes after cycling in different electrolyte to observe their SEI layers. It is found that the transparent coating layers can be observed on all the electrode surface, in contrast to the smooth surface of HC shown in Fig. S9, indicates the formation of SEI layers [28]. The SEI layers generated in G1 and G2 are notably more uniform and exhibit closer contact with the HC surface compared to those generated in G3 and G4. This enhanced uniformity and adherence provides effective protection for the electrode and ensure stable electrochemical performance for sodium storage [29,30]. To ascertain the chemical composition of the SEI layers, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses were performed on cycled HC electrodes. Variations in peak intensities and binding energies were analyzed to distinguish the inorganic and organic components of the SEI layers formed in different electrolytes. Fig. 3g displays the C 1 s, O 1 s, and F 1 s spectra of the SEI layer formed in G1. Deconvolution of the C 1 s spectrum reveals four peaks at approximately 289.4 (RCO₃), 286.3 (C=O), 283.8 (C-O), and 283.4 (C-C/C-H) eV, indicative of decomposed products of sodium salts, solvent-induced polymerizations, polyethylene oxide oligomers, and polyolefin, respectively [11,31].

The cathode electrodes were then washed with DME solvent five times to remove the residual salts followed by evaporation of DME solvent in the vacuum chamber of the glove box for at least 2 h. The electrolyte was 1 M $NaPF_{6}$ dissolved in diglyme and 1 M $NaClO_{4}$ in EC/DEC, V/V: 1:1. Before the preparation of the electrolyte, the salts were dried at 120 °C for 24 h in the vacuum chamber of the glove box. The solvents were dried using 4 Å molecular sieves for 48 h in the glove box. Electrochemical Measurements: Half-cell was assembled using a Na metal, a piece of Celgard 2325 separator, a piece of Whatman glass fiber separator (GF/C), 40 $\mu$ l electrolyte, spacer, and gasket in CR2032-type coin-cell. For the cathode, the testing voltage window was 2.7–3.8 or 1–3.8 V versus Na/Na $^{+}$ under different C-rate (1 C = 117 mAh g $^{-1}$ ). citations.quote: The HC//NFPP full cell shows stable cycling performance over 100 cycles with a high average CE (Figure S12, Supporting Information), indicating the high combability of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte in the full cells. An Ah-level HC//NFPP pouch cells were further assembled to test the feasibility of the practical application of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte. The HC//NFPP pouch cell delivers a reversible capacity of 1.029 Ah and ICE of 82.5% (Figure 3a). Meanwhile, the pouch cell exhibits excellent cycling stability with no swelling during the cycling process. Specifically, the pouch cell manifests a high capacity retention of 80% after 500 cycles at a current rate of 1 C, along with a high average CE of 99.9% (Figure 3b). Moreover, the pouch cell shows stable performance at different temperatures. The discharge capacities are 0.985, 0.884, and 1.06 Ah at -20, -40, and 60 °C (0.1 C), corresponding to 95.7%, 85.9%, and 103% of the capacity retention, respectively (Figure 3c). Even at a higher discharge rate of 0.5 C at 60 °C, the battery can still maintain 103% of its capacity at 25 °C (Figure S13, Supporting Information). The HC//NFPP pouch cell shows outstanding cycling stability at -20 and 60 °C with high capacity retention over hundreds of cycles (Figure 3d,e; Figure S14, Supporting Information). These results indicated the high combability of NaDFOB-G2 electrolytes for practical pouch cells.

To show the potential for low-temperature application, the NFPP electrodes with different electrolytes were tested at low temperatures. Notably, the NFPP electrode with NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte exhibits a capacity retention of 92.7% at -20 °C compared to that at 25 °C. Even at -40 °C, a high capacity retention of 84.8% is achieved (Figure 2g,h). Impressively, the NFPP electrode with the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte retains higher capacity retention than that with $NaPF_{6}-G2$ electrolyte at both -20 and -40 °C (Figures S6 and S7, Supporting Information). Moreover, the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte works well with other cathode materials. Both the $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}}$ electrodes show high cycling stability over 200 cycles (Figures S8 and S9, Supporting Information). Additionally, the compatibility of the NaDFOB-G2 electrolyte with the hard carbon (HC) anode is also evaluated. The HC electrode has a large overpotential at room temperature and shows a small capacity (Figure S10, Supporting Information), which may be result of the thick SEI film on the Na metal surface slowing down the speed of sodium-ions passing through the SEI film and increase the polarization of the cell (Figure S11, Supporting Information). $^{[8]}$

To avoid the influence of the high polarization from Na metal, HC//NFPP full coin-cells were assembled.

citations.quote: In summary, we developed a synthetic strategy combining a molten-salt method with a vacuum infiltration process to successfully construct a $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC composite with an $Nb-N_{4}$ coordination structure, which was employed as an anode for SIBs. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that $NaPF_{6}$ in an ether-based electrolyte (DME) more effectively promotes the electrochemical performance of electrode materials compared to ester-based electrolytes. The $Nb-N_{4}$ configuration regulates the microstructure and charge distribution of NC, significantly enhancing the pseudocapacitive behavior of $Na^{+}$ storage and enabling fast reaction kinetics. Further investigations and DFT calculations reveal the storage mechanism: the $Nb-N_{4}$ structure promotes the formation of a stable, uniform SEI layer rich in inorganic NaF by lowering the dissociation energy of P—F and C—O bonds in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME electrolyte, thereby improving specific capacity, rate performance, and cycling stability at both room and low temperatures. The optimized $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC exhibits remarkable cycling stability of 238 mAh g $^{-1}$ surpassing 3000 cycles at 10 C (25°C) and exceptional low-temperature capacity of 203 mAh g $^{-1}$ (0°C) and 130 mAh g $^{-1}$ (-20°C) at 2 C. In practical applications, a full cell assembled with NVPF cathode and $Nb_{0.03}$ -NC anode achieves an energy density of 230 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and a power density of 6.69 kW kg $^{-1}$ .

In contrast, the electrostatic potential range of DME in the $NaPF_{6}$ -DME system ranges from -1.48 eV (blue, negative charge) to 0.81 eV (red, positive charge). Compared with ester-based solvents, DME exhibits a much smaller variation in electrostatic potential and a more homogeneous charge distribution.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to calculate the average coordination number of $Na^{+}$ in the ether-based and ester-based electrolytes (Figure 2e–g). According to the radial distribution function (RDF) analysis, in the $NaPF_{6}$ in EC/EMC/DMC system, $Na^{+}$ preferentially coordinates with the oxygen atoms (O) of the solvents (EC/EMC/DMC), forming an inner solvation sheath. The cathodes exhibited an average mass loading of 15 mg cm $^{-2}$ and a tap density of 2.95 g cc $^{-1}$ . The anodes consisting of hard carbon (HC) as the active material, electrical conductor, and binder in a mass ratio of 95.3:1:3.7 were coated onto Al foil, achieving an average mass loading of 8.2 mg cm $^{-2}$ and a tap density of 0.95 g cc $^{-1}$ . Notably, the width and length of the anodes were designed to be 0.1 mm larger than those of the cathodes to ensure proper alignment and prevent short circuits. To construct the pouch cells, the cathodes and anodes were interleaved layer-by-layer, separated by a 20 $\mu$ m poly(ethylene) (PE) membrane. The assembled cell was then sealed in a laminated aluminum film bag. For the baseline electrolyte, we employed an electrolyte formulation with certain engineering application value based on prior research conducted by our group. $^{30}$ The specific formulation is as follows: 16.7954 g of NaPF $_{6}$ was dissolved in a 100 mL solvent mixture comprising propylene carbonate (PC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) in a volume ratio of 50:47:3, supplemented with 2 wt % 1,3,2-dioxathiolane-2,2-dioxide (DTD) as an additive. The optimized electrolytes were prepared by adding an appropriate amount of the PFPN additive.

citations.quote:
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

citations.quote: Despite significant advancements in the use of phosphorus-containing electrolytes and additives in laboratory research, their specific mechanisms of action in practical batteries remain poorly understood. $^{25,26}$ This knowledge gap highlights the need for further research to elucidate the mechanisms of performance enhancement by phosphorus-containing components, especially in SIBs, which is critical for advancing their commercialization. $^{27}$ Among these components, ethoxy (pentafluoro) cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN) has been widely utilized as an additive to enhance battery safety. $^{28,29}$ In this study, PFPN was introduced into practical pouch-cell-type SIBs to evaluate its effects on cycling performance and capacity optimization under various temperature conditions, thereby redefining the application potential of PFPN additives. These results demonstrate that PFPN significantly improves the low-temperature electrochemical performance of SIBs. Specifically, the incorporation of 10 wt % PFPN enables the battery to retain 85% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at a 0.2 C rate at 0 °C. During electrochemical cycling, PFPN facilitates the formation of a unique SEI layer enriched with phosphorus and nitrogen elements, which improves the kinetic performance of the battery.

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Low-temperature cyclability is one of the key advantages of sodium-ion batteries. However, reduced kinetics at low temperatures hinder the efficient intercalation of sodium ions into hard carbon, leading to metallic sodium deposition on electrode surfaces, which results in capacity degradation and safety concerns. To address this issue, we investigated the effects of the PFPN additive on low-temperature performance using a 0.4 Ah-level NFM-HC pouch cell. The cells underwent a formation process at a 0.1 C rate, as shown in the formation curves in Figure S1. The charge and discharge curves of both cells were nearly identical. Subsequent EIS analysis after formation revealed that cells with the electrolyte containing 10 wt % PFPN exhibited lower resistance (Figure 1a), indicating that the PFPN additive effectively reduces interfacial resistance in the cells.

The low-temperature cyclability of cells with the baseline electrolyte and 10 wt % PFPN additive was evaluated at 0 °C and 0.2 C rate (Figure 1b–d). Notably, the cell with 10 wt % PFPN additive demonstrated approximately 4% higher capacity retention compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%) after 450 cycles (Figure 1b). During cycling, the average Coulombic efficiency of the baseline electrolyte was 99.939%, whereas the electrolyte containing 10 wt % PFPN achieved 99.951%. Although the charge–discharge curves (Figure 1c) did not immediately reveal significant differences between the electrolytes, the differential voltage curves (Figure S2) highlighted distinct behaviors. 4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, the incorporation of PFPN as an electrolyte additive has successfully led to significant enhancements in both the low-temperature performance of sodium-ion batteries and the flame retardancy of the electrolyte. The NFM-HC pouch cell with 10 wt % PFPN exhibited a capacity retention of 85% after 450 cycles at 0.2 C rate and 0 °C, representing an approximate 4% increase in capacity compared to the baseline electrolyte (81.33%), and a capacity retention of 84% after 600 cycles at 0.5 C and 30 °C. This improvement is attributed to the formation of a SEI layer rich in P and N elements on the electrode surface. The SEI layer is thinner and possesses superior kinetic properties compared to the baseline, effectively preventing sodium plating and enhancing the cycle life. This research highlights the potential of PFPN in sodium ion battery applications requiring long-life and low-temperature operation, offering new insights into electrolyte modification using P- and F-containing additives.

citations.quote: Coin cells (CR2032) were used to test the electrochemical performances. 1M NaClO $_{4}$ solution in a mixture of ethylene carbonate/propylene carbonate (EC/PC) (1:1 in volume) was applied as the electrolyte for the half cell and full cells. Two pieces of Whatman glass fibers soaked with the electrolyte were used as the separator between the positive and negative electrode. The HC electrode was prepared by casting a slurry of 90 wt% HC, 5 wt% conductive carbon black and 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder on copper foil. In companions, electrodes using carboxymethylcellulose sodium salt (CMC) and sodium alginate (NaAg) as the binder were also prepared. Typical loading mass of the HC electrode was around 1.5 mg cm $^{-2}$ . For the full cell, Na $_{3.5}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{2}$ F $_{3}$ powders were mixed with 20% carbon SP for the preparation of positive electrodes. The weight ratio of the positive/negative electrodes was 2.5. The cells were galvanostatic charged/discharged with a LAND 2001 CT battery test system (Wuhan, China) under various voltage ranges and current rates. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a VMP system (Biologic S.A., Claix, France).

citations.quote:
Conclusion
In summary, a hard carbon material for NIBs is fabricated from low-cost biomass waste using a facile two-step thermal treatment. Compared to direct high-temperature carbonization, the pre-treatment at a medium temperature is beneficial to avoiding the selfactivation effect of impurities. An appropriate surface area and pore size distribution are obtained, enabling a stable capacity of around 300 mAh g $^{-1}$ . It also shows excellent performance at a temperature as low as -20 °C. A safe and reversible capacity of 250 mAh g $^{-1}$ can be obtained without Na plating at -20 °C, as evidenced by in situ XRD and Raman tests. As-prepared HC also delivers stable performance in the full cell coupling with a $\mathrm{Na}_{3.5}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{2}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ cathode, demonstrated an energy density of 310 Wh kg $^{-1}$ (based on the total weight of electrode) with decent cyclic stability at room temperature. Nevertheless, the full cell shows a fast capacity fading at -20 °C due to both the increased resistance and continuous consumption of Na ions. It calls for building stable SEI under low temperature in future studies.

From the calculation, the diffusion coefficient of Na-ions ( $D_{Na}^{+}$ ) at 25°C is in the range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10}$ cm $^{2}$ s $^{-1}$ . The value is only slightly decreased at 0°C. In sharp contrast, the $D_{Na}^{+}$ value is about one magnitude lower at -25 °C than that at 25°C. The slow $Na^{+}$ diffusion is in agreement with the EIS results that the thicker SEI film would affect the ion diffusion. After testing at $-20^{\circ}C$ for 10 cycles, the same cell (F3) was put back to $25^{\circ}C$ and its capacity gradually recovered and regained ca. 82% of the capacity at $25^{\circ}C$ .

To evaluate the impacts of NVPF microstructure on the cyclic stability for achieving remarkable long cycle life, the von mises stress distribution of solid NVPF sphere and nanosheet-assembled NVPF sphere were calculated by COMSOL finite element simulation in Fig. 1a. A robust inorganic-rich NaF and $\mathrm{NaB_xO_y}$ species CEI layer on HM-NVPF@CN surface was spontaneous formed in the dual-salt ether electrolyte (0.8 M $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ and 0.2 M $\mathrm{NaBF_4}$ in DEGDME, denoted as BPG). The electrochemical performance was tested by CR2032 coin-type. citations.quote:
ABSTRACT
$Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{2}F_{3}$ (denoted as NVPF) is an attractive cathode for sodium ion batteries (NIB) owning to its high theoretical capacity (128 mAh g $^{-1}$ ) and high working potential (3.9 V vs Na/Na $^{+}$ ). However, NVPF often suffers from low electronic conductivity and unstable cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI), seriously hindering its practical application. Here, a uniform NVPF microsphere assembled by carbon-coated NVPF nanosheets (HM-NVPF@CN) is prepared and subsequently an inorganic-rich B, F species CEI layer on its surface in dual-anion ether electrolyte is constructed to address above drawbacks. The carbon-coated NVPF nanosheets can shorten the diffusion pathway for both Na $^{+}$ and e $^{-}$ , and provide large electrochemical reaction area. In addition, the robust CEI layer can enhance the Na $^{+}$ transport and suppress the parasitic reactions. The optimized electrode exhibits a good cycling stability (70 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 2000 cycles) and outstanding low temperature performance (99 mAh g $^{-1}$ at -25 °C). The full cell fabricated with a hard carbon (HC) anode achieves a high capacity retention (88% after 930 cycles) and superior high temperature performance (60 °C, 72 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 5C). This work provides a novel idea to regulate interfacial chemistry of cathodes for the high-voltage NIB.

citations.quote: For example, $NaClO_{4}$ is very explosive and its adsorbed $H_{2}O$ is too difficult to dry out. $^{[28]}$ $NaPF_{6}$ is toxic and expensive, easy to decompose at elevated temperatures and under humidity. $^{[5,14]}$ The NaTFSI and NaFSI are of high cost, and the $TFSI^{-}$ (or $FSI^{-}$ ) anion in NaTFSI (or NaFSI) has a corrosive effect on the aluminum foil collector. $^{[8]}$ Thus, it is of great significance to explore advanced salts to promote the wide applicability of SIBs. Sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB), which has non-localized electrons in the structure and weak bonds between sodium-ions and anions, has shown fascinating properties, such as high conductivity, compatibility with a variety of solvents, and own film-forming characteristics with no need for film-forming additives. $^{[14,29,30]}$ However, the use of NaDFOB as a single salt for electrolytes and their compatibility with different SIB electrodes have rarely been reported.

citations.chunk_id: 0070_Xia 等 - 2025 - Sodium-DifluorooxalatoBorate-Based Electrolytes for Long-Term Cycle Life and Enhanced Low-Temperat::sec0::child0
citations.quote:
Miaomiao Xia, Hui Chen, Zhenxu Zheng, Qingfei Meng, $^{*}$ Along Zhao, Xiaoyang Chen, Xinping Ai, Yongjin Fang, $^{*}$ and Yuliang Cao $^{*}$

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are emerging as a promising alternative for next-generation energy storage solutions, driven by the economic and environmental benefits of abundant sodium resources. A pivotal aspect of SIB advancement is the development of advanced electrolytes, which remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a facile and scalable synthesis method for low-cost sodium-difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) is reported and explored its application as a standalone electrolyte salt for SIBs. The NaDFOB-based ether electrolyte demonstrates exceptional electrochemical stability, solvent compatibility, and the unique capacity to form a dense, robust solid-electrolyte interphase layer on electrode surfaces. As a result, the $\mathrm{Na_{4}Fe_{3}(PO_{4})_{2}P_{2}O_{7}}$ (NFPP) cathode with NaDFOB-based electrolyte exhibits ultrahigh cycling stability with a remarkable capacity retention of 98.7% after 1000 cycles. Furthermore, an Ah-level hard carbon (HC)//NFPP pouch cell using NaDFOB-based ether electrolyte shows an impressive cycle life of 500 cycles, coupled with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.9%. citations.quote: Overall, an unprecedented high-power-density rechargeable NVP||HC full battery has been realized at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ without Na plating on HC anode surface, which can be attributed to the following three aspects: a) the designed high-solvation-entropy electrolyte (1 M $NaPF_{6}$ -G2/DME) with a small solvation cluster size possesses elevated ionic conductivity and larger $t_{Na}^{+}$ value at low temperatures compared with conventional electrolytes, facilitating $Na^{+}$ migration to the HC surface; b) a thin, NaF-rich SEI layer with small interfacial resistance is generated on the HC anode surface in the designed electrolyte, promoting $Na^{+}$ transport through the SEI; c) fast kinetics lowers the electrochemical polarization, hence suppressing Na plating on the HC anode.

3. Conclusion
In conclusion, we successfully realize a high-power-density rechargeable sodium-ion full battery operated at $-40\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ without Na plating by rational electrolyte modulation. 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -G2/DME electrolyte with small solvation clusters size was designed, enabling high $\sigma$ and t $_{\text{Na}}^{+}$ at low temperatures. Notably, the enhanced CIP structure of the designed electrolyte induces the formation of a thin, anion-derived NaF-rich SEI layer on HC anode with small interfacial resistance, facilitating facile Na $^{+}$ transport through the SEI. As a result, the HC anode in the designed electrolyte presents a remarkably high capacity of 284 mAh g $^{-1}$ (0.06 A g $^{-1}$ ) and 97 mAh g $^{-1}$ (2.10 A g $^{-1}$ ) at $-40\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ , respectively. Impressively, the NVP||HC full battery achieves a record-high power density of 1132.31 W kg $^{-1}$ (with an energy density of 61.94 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) at $-40\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and exhibits an outstanding capacity retention of 80.60% over 1400 cycles at $-40\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ . This work would facilitate the development of low-temperature SIBs for practical power-intensive application scenarios.

citations.quote: As the most promising anode material for commercialization in SIBs, hard carbon (HC) possesses a low-potential plateau ( $\approx0.1\ V$ ) with a high capacity, which is favorable for increasing the energy density of full batteries. $^{[21-24]}$ Nevertheless, at low temperatures and high rates, the operating potential of HC can easily drop below 0 V versus $Na^{+}/Na$ due to the increased electrochemical impedance and polarization, inducing undesirable Na plating on HC anode. $^{[25,26]}$ Therefore, it remains arduous to realize high-power-density HC-based SIBs at low temperatures. Herein, a high-power-density rechargeable HC-based sodium-ion full battery is successfully realized at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ through rational electrolyte chemistry (Scheme 1). Benefited from the high entropy and small solvation clusters of the designed electrolyte, high ionic conductivity and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ transference number $(\mathrm{t_{Na}^{+}})$ can be achieved at low temperatures. Significantly, the enhanced contact-ion pairs in the designed electrolyte induce the formation of a thin, NaF-rich SEI layer on HC anode with small interfacial resistance. When paired with $\mathrm{Na}_3\mathrm{V}_2(\mathrm{PO}_4)_3$ (NVP), the full bat tery demonstrates a record-high power density of 1132.31 W kg $^{-1}$ (with an energy density of 61.94 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) at -40 °C without Na plating. This work sheds light on future development of low-temperature, high-power-density batteries.

Yingyu Wang, Hao Lan, Shuai Dong, Qiaonan Zhu, Liwei Cheng, Han Wang, Jiawei Wang, Sicong Wang, Mengyao Tang, Kurbanov Mirtemir Shodievich, Gongkai Wang, and Hua Wang\*

High-power-density rechargeable batteries are highly indispensable for power-intensive application scenarios, such as vehicle start-stop system and grid-level frequency regulation. However, realizing high-power-density alkali-ion batteries is challenging especially at low temperatures, as undesirable alkali metal plating tends to occur more easily on the anode surface due to the increased electrochemical impedance and polarization. Herein, a low-temperature, high-power-density rechargeable $Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ ||hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion full battery without Na plating is realized by electrolyte regulation. The designed high-solvation-entropy electrolyte enables a high ionic conductivity of 13.87 mS cm $^{-1}$ at -40 °C. More importantly, the enhanced contact-ion pairs solvation structure induces an anion-derived, thin, NaF-rich solid electrolyte interface (SEI) on HC anodes with low interfacial resistance to ensure facile $Na^{+}$ diffusion through the SEI. Consequently, the assembled sodium-ion full battery demonstrates a record-high power density of 1132.31 W kg $^{-1}$ (with an energy density of 61.94 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) at -40 °C and 13372.56 W kg $^{-1}$ (132.83 Wh kg $^{-1}$ ) at 25 °C (based on total mass of the active materials on anode and cathode).

Abstract Hard carbon (HC) remains the most commercially viable anode for sodium-ion batteries, yet its low initial Coulombic efficiency and unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) hinder long-term performance. Electrolyte engineering offers a promising strategy to regulate SEI chemistry, enhancing interfacial $Na^{+}$ transport and interphase stability. However, the respective roles of solvents and anions in tailoring the SEI on HC remain elusive. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that weak $Na^{+}-G2$ interactions permit more anions to enter the primary solvation shell, facilitating the formation of an inorganic-rich SEI that promotes high ionic conductivity and redox kinetics. Additionally, the preferential decomposition of $OTF^{-}$ -anions results in a uniform and robust SEI. As a result, HC anodes cycled in NaOTF-G2 deliver a reversible specific capacity of $\sim200\ mAh\ g^{-1}$ over 3000 cycles. Furthermore, a $\mathrm{Na}_{3}\mathrm{V}_{2}(\mathrm{PO}_{4})_{3}||\mathrm{HC}$ pouch cell incorporating this optimized electrolyte achieves a capacity retention of 81% at $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ . citations.quote: In summary, a series of electrolytes (1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ -EC/DMC, 1.0 M $NaPF_{6}$ -G2, and 1.0 M NaOTF-G2 electrolytes) was chosen in this study to investigate the separate effects of salt and solvent on $Na^{+}$ storage mechanisms in hard carbon anodes at a wide range of temperatures. The weak interaction between $Na^{+}$ and G2 allows more anions to enter the $Na^{+}$ solvation shell and forms the anion-derived robust and inorganic-rich interphase. This interface satisfies ion conductivity and facilitates a high $Na^{+}$ transference number, with superior redox kinetics in ether-based solvents, leading to excellent rate performance. Moreover, the preferential decomposition of OTF $^{-}$ -anions induces a highly uniform and ultrahigh inorganic-rich SEI, inhibiting side reactions and enhancing ICE as well as extending cycle lifespan. The HC using NaOTF-G2 electrolyte delivers an ideal ICE of 89.8% and achieves a specific capacity of 283.0 mAh g $^{-1}$ after 100 cycles. Even at -40 °C, the NVP | | HC full pouch cell still maintains approximately 81% of its excellent specific capacity after 100 cycles. This work provides a novel and universal electrolyte design strategy to optimize the electrochemical behavior of electrode materials by targeting the roles of solvents and anions.

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.
