citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec6::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we present a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte that is compatible with high $Na^{+}$ desolvation rates for SIBs by regulating solvation structure. Due to the weakened ion-dipole interaction of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL has a low-temperature responsive solvation structure. As the temperature decreases, solvent coordination reduces and anion coordination increases in the first solvated shell of $Na^{+}$ . The temperature-sensitive solvation structure accelerates the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ , mitigating the voltage polarization on the HC surface. This enables HC to achieve higher capacity retention at high current density and low temperatures, thereby enhancing the low-temperature performance of SIBs. The HC anode realized a high capacity of 220.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -40 °C, with 91.9% capacity retention after 900 cycles. At -30 °C, the capacity retention rate of HC||NVP pouch cell after 100 cycles at 0.1 C is 92.43%, indicating that electrolytes with low-temperature adaptation can effectively improve the low-temperature performance of SIBs. Noteworthy, temperature-adapted solvation structures universally exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes, which have exceedingly outstanding low-temperature performance. This provides a new way for designing low-temperature sodium-ion batteries and broadens their application for energy storage in extremely cold regions.

citations.quote: The Na+-MP complex exhibits a low binding energy (-1.38 eV), consistent with its low DN value, further validating the weak coordination ability of MP. The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

citations.chunk_id: 0004_Chang 等 - 2025 - Solvent-Fluorine-Free Anion-Enriched and Non-Flammable Electrolyte Enables Safe Sodium-Ion Battery::sec6::child0
citations.quote: To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle).

citations.quote: The XPS results of the HC anode reveal a higher proportion of inorganic NaF species in NTM system (Figures S38 and S39, Supporting Information). With increasing sputtering time, NaF gradually becomes the dominant component, forming a bilayer solid-electrolyte interlayer (SEI) structure consisting of an inorganic-rich inner layer and an organic-rich outer layer. In summary, these results confirm that the NTM electrolyte simultaneously constructs NaF-rich and stable interfaces on both the NVP cathode and HC anode within full cells. The synergistic optimization of both cathode and anode interfaces is the fundamental origin of the battery's excellent electrochemical performance. Furthermore, the high- and low-temperature electrochemical performance of the electrolytes was evaluated in full-cell configurations. The results reveal that the NTM system retains 67.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ (77.8% retention) after 100 cycles at 50 °C, whereas the NP system exhibits only 61.7% retention with more pronounced fading (Figure 5f; Figure S40, Supporting Information). The NTM system also demonstrates stable cycling behavior at 80 °C (Figure S41, Supporting Information). This enhanced stability primarily arises from the formation of NaF-enriched gradient CEI/SEI layers, which effectively suppress electrolyte decomposition at elevated temperatures.

citations.quote:
4. Conclusions
In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively. In short, the designed electrolyte enriches the SIBs applied in low temperatures, paving the way for further application of carboxylate ester-based electrolytes.

citations.quote: To solve the problem of sluggish ion mobility in the electrode materials at low temperatures, NASICON-type NVPOF with high intrinsic ion diffusion was selected as the cathode material to verify the availability of the designed MP-based electrolyte at sub-zero temperature operation. The preparation process, structure, and morphology characterization of the micron-size NVPOF were shown in the experimental section and Fig. S4, according to our previous work [42]. To confirm, the Na||NVPOF half-cells with different electrolytes were assembled to investigate the electrochemical performance at the temperature range from 25 to $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in the voltage window of $2.5 - 4.3\mathrm{V}$ (vs. $\mathrm{Na^{+} / Na}$ ). At $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) curves of the NVPOF electrode using two electrolytes are basically the same (Fig. 2(a)) except for the slight difference in the first coulombic efficiency, which means that the two electrolytes are well matched to the NVPOF cathode. citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.quote:
2.4. Electrochemical Performance of Full Cell
We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). Surprisingly, it can operate normally at LT, and specifically preserve a capacity of 79.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at $-40$ °C, which is equivalent to 80.0% of the capacity at 25 °C in Figure S25 (Supporting Information). This indicates that temperature-adaptive electrolytes are not only compatible with NVP, but can also upgrade the rate performance and low-temperature performance of NVP cathode.

To further verify the feasibility of electrolytes in SIBs, the coin full cell with NVP cathode and pre-cycled HC anode was assembled and subjected to rate performance testing at 25 °C. It displays that the full cell coupled with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can still retain a capacity of 71.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while the cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 can only bestow a capacity of 52.3 mAh g $^{-1}$ in Figure 6a. Additionally, the performance of the full cell was evaluated at -40 °C and it was manifested that the full cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can preserve 64.8% of its capacity at 25 °C in Figure 6b. After 50 cycles of 0.1 C (10 mA g $^{-1}$ ) at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 95.7%, and then after 50 cycles of 0.1 C at -40 °C, the capacity retention rate was 92.8%, as shown in Figure 6c. To test the practical application of electrolytes, a piece pouch cell (45 mAh) was assembled for cycling testing in Figure 6d and Figure S26 (Supporting Information). After cycling 100 cycles at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 86.7%. Then, the pouch cell was cycled 100 cycles at -30 °C, and the capacity retention rate was 92.43% in Figure 6e. Therefore, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL electrolyte with a temperature-adaptive solvent structure holds great potential in the practical application of SIBs.

citations.quote:
Yuewei Cui, Youxuan Ni, Yuankun Wang, Linyue Wang, Wenxuan Yang, Shuang Wu, Weiwei Xie, Kai Zhang, Zhenhua Yan,\* and Jun Chen\*

Sodium-ion batteries are applied to cold-resistant energy storage hindered by phase transitions and sluggish $Na^{+}$ migration of traditional carbonate-based electrolytes at low temperatures. The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

citations.quote:
Yuewei Cui, Youxuan Ni, Yuankun Wang, Linyue Wang, Wenxuan Yang, Shuang Wu, Weiwei Xie, Kai Zhang, Zhenhua Yan,\* and Jun Chen\*

Sodium-ion batteries are applied to cold-resistant energy storage hindered by phase transitions and sluggish $Na^{+}$ migration of traditional carbonate-based electrolytes at low temperatures. The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec2::child0
citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.quote: To quantitatively elucidate the solvation structure of the two electrolytes, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed at 25 °C. The radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure 2e,f displays the distribution of each component around $Na^{+}$ in two electrolytes at 25 °C. The average coordination number (CN) values of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) in 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 and 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL are 5.979 and 4.733, respectively. The CN of Na–F ( $PF_{6}^{-}$ ) increases from 0.233 to 1.092, as shown in Figure 2g and Table S1 (Supporting Information). This indeed indicates that DOL weakens the coordination oxygen activity of G2, thereby reducing the coordination of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) and increasing the coordination of anions. The phase transition temperatures of the two electrolytes were evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and cryopolarizing microscope. Remarkably, the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is $-91$ °C, while the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 is only $-46$ °C, as shown in Figure 2h. Moreover, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 generates small ice crystals at $-50$ °C and emerges a large-scale phase transition at $-70$ °C. 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is a pure liquid at $-50$ °C and solvent crystallization does not occur until it is cooled to $-110$ °C (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Variable temperature viscosity tests were conducted on these two electrolytes in Figure 2i.

citations.quote: As the most commonly used electrolyte for SIBs, a PC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -PC/FEC was used as the control (hereafter referred to as PC) [42,43]. Similarly, the proposed carboxylate ester-based electrolytes in this work are composed of MP, FEC, and NaPF $_{6}$ . Firstly, the influence of concentration on electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte was investigated, and as shown in Fig. S1(a), the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte with 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ is significantly higher than that of the electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ . Moreover, the MP-based electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ has better electrochemical stability (Fig. S1(b)), therefore 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ -MP/FEC was selected for research, which will be referred to as MP in the following. The redox reaction activities of isolated solvents and sodium salt of MP and PC-based electrolytes are investigated with frontier molecular orbital theory, involving the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels (Fig. 1(a)). The LUMO/HOMO energy level of MP is close to PC, which indicates MP has considerable oxidation/reduction stability compared to PC. In addition, the HOMO level of FEC is lower than that of the other solvents, indicating the stronger capability of the free fluorinated carbonate solvent against oxidation.

citations.chunk_id: 0038_Liu 等 - 2024 - Ester-based anti-freezing electrolyte achieving ultra-low temperature cycling for sodium-ion batteri::sec11::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively.

The assembled HC||NVPOF full cells exhibit a high discharging specific capacity of 119.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C, and the GCD profiles are shown in Fig. 6(b), which overlap well in the first five cycles, suggesting the excellent reversibility of the HC||NVPOF full cells. The HC||NVPOF full cells also exhibit superior cycling performance, as shown in Fig. 6(d), at the rate of 0.5 C, the HC||NVPOF full cells achieve a high average coulombic efficiency (CE) of 99.6% and maintain 98.2% capacity retention after 150 cycles. citations.quote: The Na+-MP complex exhibits a low binding energy (-1.38 eV), consistent with its low DN value, further validating the weak coordination ability of MP. The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

The intermolecular forces between MP and TEP, along with changes in the electrolyte's solvation structure, were further confirmed through Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy. As depicted in Figure 2b, the split peaks at 1268 cm $^{-1}$ in pure TEP solvent correspond to the P=O stretching vibrations of TEP in the C $_{3\nu}$ and C $_{3}$ conformers, respectively. $^{[36,37]}$ In the NT system, however, the splitting characteristics of the P=O peak disappear and exhibit a significant downshift upon the introduction of NaPF $_{6}$ . This phenomenon is attributed to the formation of the Na $^{+}$ -TEP $_{P=O}$ complex, which modifies the vibration of the P=O bond.

citations.quote: To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle).

citations.quote:
2.5. Toward Practical Viability
To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle). In contrast, the NTM system exhibits a smaller capacity loss, achieving a retention of 95.3% (Figure 5e). Additionally, the NTM system displays a smaller voltage drop during the static period (Figure S35, Supporting Information). These findings suggest that the NTM electrolyte effectively mitigates side reactions, likely due to the formation of a stable interfacial film that suppresses electrolyte decomposition.

XPS was further employed to investigate the interfacial layers of the NVP cathode and HC anode in the cycled full cells. As shown in Figure S36 (Supporting Information, NVP cathode side), the electrode cycled in the NTM electrolyte exhibits lower C and O elemental contents but higher Na and F elemental contents on the surface compared with the NP electrolyte. citations.quote: The liquid temperature range of the electrolyte determines the battery's operational capability across a wide temperature range. Particularly at extremely low temperatures, the electrolyte's antifreezing properties are critical to ensuring battery operability. $^{[44]}$ Digital photographs show that the NTM electrolyte retains good fluidity without phase transition even when the temperature drops to $-60\ ^{\circ}C$ , thereby demonstrating superior anti-freezing properties (Figure S21, Supporting Information). Figures 4a and S22 (Supporting Information) show that the NP electrolyte shows a sharp decline in ionic conductivity below $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ due to the high viscosity of PC. In contrast, the NTM electrolyte exhibits superior ionic conductivity across the entire temperature range, particularly at sub-zero conditions, and exhibits lower activation energies for ion transport from $50\ ^{\circ}C$ to $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ (1.24 and 2.00 kJ mol $^{-1}$ vs. 2.00 and 3.04 kJ mol $^{-1}$ for NT vs. 2.32 and 4.91 kJ mol $^{-1}$ for NP). Notably, at $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ , the NTM electrolyte retains an ionic conductivity of 1.4 mS cm $^{-1}$ , significantly higher than those of NT (0.27 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) and NP (0.23 mS cm $^{-1}$ ), as detailed in Table S2 (Supporting Information).

In addition, the NVP||HC full cell employing the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 100 cycles under the extreme conditions of high voltage (4.3 V) and 50 °C (Figure S42, Supporting Information). The NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte exhibits remarkable temperature adaptability across a broad temperature range. At low temperatures of -20 and -40 °C, the NTM-based electrolyte still delivers high discharge capacities of 71.5 mA h g $^{-1}$ and 62.2 mA h g $^{-1}$ , corresponding to 83.2% and 72.4% of the discharge capacity at room temperature, respectively (Figure 5g). Additionally, the battery can stably complete 50 discharge cycles at -20 °C (Figure S43, Supporting Information), and even successfully operate for 20 cycles at -40 °C, maintaining a capacity retention rate of 83.9% (Figure 5h; Figure S44, Supporting Information). Benefiting from the excellent anti-freezing capability and low-temperature ionic conductivity of the NTM electrolyte, the NVP||HC full cell delivers an average specific capacity of 31.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ at -60 °C (Figure S45, Supporting Information).

In addition, the NVP||HC full cell employing the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 100 cycles under the extreme conditions of high voltage (4.3 V) and 50 °C (Figure S42, Supporting Information). The NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte exhibits remarkable temperature adaptability across a broad temperature range. At low temperatures of -20 and -40 °C, the NTM-based electrolyte still delivers high discharge capacities of 71.5 mA h g $^{-1}$ and 62.2 mA h g $^{-1}$ , corresponding to 83.2% and 72.4% of the discharge capacity at room temperature, respectively (Figure 5g). Additionally, the battery can stably complete 50 discharge cycles at -20 °C (Figure S43, Supporting Information), and even successfully operate for 20 cycles at -40 °C, maintaining a capacity retention rate of 83.9% (Figure 5h; Figure S44, Supporting Information). Benefiting from the excellent anti-freezing capability and low-temperature ionic conductivity of the NTM electrolyte, the NVP||HC full cell delivers an average specific capacity of 31.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ at -60 °C (Figure S45, Supporting Information).

citations.quote: Furthermore, the NTM electrolyte enables excellent rate performance at 50 °C and even stable cycling at an extreme temperature of 80 °C (Figures S25 and S26, Supporting Information). This superior performance is attributed to the formation of a robust NaF-enriched interface and thermally stable TEP. At -40 °C, the NVP||Na cell with NP electrolyte delivers only 22.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ after 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , owing to its low ionic conductivity and sluggish ion transport. The NT-based cell fails rapidly due to partial electrolyte solidification and high ion transfer activation energy (Figure 4b). Conversely, the NVP||Na cell with NTM electrolyte delivers 64.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ and 95.6% capacity retention after 100 cycles (Figure 4d,e; Figure S27, Supporting Information), underscoring its superior competitiveness (Table S4, Supporting Information). The NTM electrolyte also exhibits high specific capacities at various current rates even under the extremely low temperature of -40 °C, delivering 80.0, 72.3, 62.7, and 51.6 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 10, 20, 50, and 100 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure S28, Supporting Information).

citations.quote: To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle).

reviews.reason: The candidate's NaPF6/DIG-based ether electrolyte matches an electrolyte demonstrated at -40°C with good capacity retention, but all such evidence is on NTP||NVP cells (up to 1.2 Ah), so the target HC||NVP and 45 mAh cell identity remain unverified; I therefore hold rather than issue a recommendation pending HC||NVP-specific evidence.
reviews.association: The NaPF6 ether electrolyte and its -40°C performance (93.1% retention after 180 cycles at 0.1 C) are measured on NTP||NVP cells and a 1 Ah-level NTP||NVP pouch, not on the target HC||NVP 45 mAh cell; because the anode and cell capacity differ, the paper does not establish a transfer of this retention result to the HC||NVP target, so the electrolyte chemistry is supported but the candidate's specific target cell is not.

citations.quote: Fig. 5h compares the wide-temperature performance of NTP||NVP full cells with other reported sodium-ion batteries in terms of actual capacity (AC) to theoretical capacity (TC) ratio at different temperatures [44,47–50]. To further prove the fast-charging and widely operated performance of NTP||NVP sodium-ion battery system, we assembled a 1 Ah-level sodium-ion pouch cell. As shown in Fig. 6a, the pouch cell was composed of cathode (NVP), anode (NTP), separators (polypropylene-polyethylene composite), tabs (Al), electrolyte (1 M NaPF $_{6}$ in DIGYDME) and shell (aluminum-plastic composite film). The detailed parameters of NTP||NVP pouch cell was shown in Table S5. As shown in Fig. 6b, the pouch cell showed a reversible capacity of 1.2 Ah with an average working potential of 1.2 V (insert the picture of pouch cell) under room temperature. The rate capability of this pouch was shown in Fig. 6c, which exhibited a reversible capacity of 1.21 Ah, 1.17 Ah, 1.11 Ah, 1.04 Ah, 1.01 Ah, and 0.95 Ah, at 0.1 C, 0.3 C, 1 C, 3 C, 5 C and 10 C, respectively, with a maximum power density of 405.6 W kg $^{-1}$ . The cycle stability of this pouch cell was shown in Fig. 6d, which showed a reversible capacity of 1.21 Ah with a capacity retention ratio of 97.6 % after 50th cycles at 0.1 C.

citations.quote: As depicted in Fig. 5a, the NTP||NVP full cell demonstrated the specific capacity of 108 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 105 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 and 0 °C, respectively. Even the test temperature decreased to -40 °C, the full cell still maintained a reversible capacity of 75 mAh g $^{-1}$ , approximately 64 % of the capacity than it at room temperature. This impressive performance can be attributed to the low freezing point of ether-based electrolytes, enabling normal operation and high capacity at -40 °C. Despite some polarization at low temperatures, the discharge plateau of the NTP anode remains above -40 °C, effectively preventing sodium precipitation and ensuring safe cell operation. The cycling stability and rate capacity of the NTP||NVP cell at -40 °C were also assessed. As shown in Fig. 5b, the cell exhibited a remarkable rate capacity at -40 °C, retaining 72 % capacity from 0.1 to 1 C. Fig. 5c shows the cycle stability of NTP||NVP full cell, which demonstrates an excellent 93.1 % capacity retention after 180 cycles at 0.1 C. Following the high/low-temperature performance evaluation, we examined the high-temperature stability of the NTP||NVP cell from 30 to 60 °C. The constant-current charge/discharge curves in Fig. 5d indicate discharge capacities of 104.6, 108, and 112.2 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 30, 40, and 50 °C, respectively. Even at 60 °C, the cell delivered a reversible discharge specific capacity of 112.4 mAh g $^{-1}$ with an average coulombic efficiency of more than 99 %.

The B $_{E}$ of the [Na-DIG] $^{+}$ -[PF $_{6}$ ] $^{-}$ complex rises slightly from -2.08 eV to -1.54 eV from 25 to -40 °C, and decreases to -2.12 eV as the temperature rises to 60 °C, whereas the B $_{E}$ of the ester-based electrolyte decreases from -1.13 eV to -1.98 eV in the -40 to 60 °C, and the ether-based electrolyte has superior solvation energy. The increase in temperature facilitates the entry of more [PF $_{6}$ ] $^{-}$ ([ClO $_{4}$ ] $^{-}$ ) into the solvated structure, and the participation in the solvation process increases the binding energy, thus stabilizing the Na $^{+}$ -solvent complex [39]. The ether-based electrolyte exhibits a gentler solvation energy change over a wide temperature range, and this temperature-adapted solvated structure with stabilized complexes can achieve higher Na-ion mobility at low temperatures, which helps to prevent the precipitation of Na.

citations.quote: As depicted in Fig. 5a, the NTP||NVP full cell demonstrated the specific capacity of 108 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 105 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 and 0 °C, respectively. Even the test temperature decreased to -40 °C, the full cell still maintained a reversible capacity of 75 mAh g $^{-1}$ , approximately 64 % of the capacity than it at room temperature. This impressive performance can be attributed to the low freezing point of ether-based electrolytes, enabling normal operation and high capacity at -40 °C. Despite some polarization at low temperatures, the discharge plateau of the NTP anode remains above -40 °C, effectively preventing sodium precipitation and ensuring safe cell operation. Even at 60 °C, the cell delivered a reversible discharge specific capacity of 112.4 mAh g $^{-1}$ with an average coulombic efficiency of more than 99 %.

reviews.reason: Candidate-1 is precisely the paper's single-salt NaPF6 'blank' electrolyte, which satisfies the collector/shell non-corrosion requirement but is the weaker low-temperature baseline: the same work shows the blank system's -20 C capacity/recovery is clearly below the 0.5 M NaFSI double-salt, and no -10 C data exist for it, so low-temperature suitability for the -10 C target is not established and the candidate is held rather than recommended.
reviews.association: The candidate's chemistry, salt, solvent ratios and pouch full-cell testing are directly matched by the paper's 'blank' 1 M NaPF6 electrolyte in NNFM111/HC pouch cells, which supports the identity of the candidate. The corrosion evidence for the Al foil and stainless-steel shell, however, comes from separate two-electrode Al/Na and stainless-steel/Na electrolytic cells, not from the pouch full cell, so it is a limited material-compatibility association rather than a full-cell corrosion demonstration.

requirements.requirement: Electrolyte salt is 1.0 M NaPF6 (single salt, no additive)
requirements.reasoning: The source's 'blank' electrolyte is exactly 1 M NaPF6, and the candidate's salt/concentration match it.

requirements.requirement: Solvent system is EC/PC/EMC/DEC in 1:2:6:1 mass ratio
requirements.reasoning: The blank electrolyte is described as EC, PC, EMC and DEC at 1:2:6:1 by weight, matching candidate-1's solvent set and mass basis.

requirements.requirement: Cell chemistry is NFM (NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2) cathode with hard-carbon anode
requirements.reasoning: The paper studies NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2/hard-carbon (NNFM111/HC) sodium-ion cells, matching the NFM||HC target.

requirements.requirement: Pouch-cell format
requirements.reasoning: The electrochemical measurements were made on pouch NNFM111/HC cells, matching the target pouch format.

requirements.requirement: No observed Al current-collector or stainless-steel shell corrosion
requirements.reasoning: For the single NaPF6 system both the aluminum foil and the stainless-steel sheets show higher stability with rapid current convergence, and the single-NaPF6 electrolyte remained clear and original after cycling, i.e. no corrosion products. Note this was observed in two-electrode Al/Na and stainless-steel/Na electrolytic cells rather than the pouch full cell.

requirements.requirement: Low-temperature operation at the target -10 C
requirements.reasoning: The source reports low-temperature data only at -20 C for the NNFM111/HC full cell, not at -10 C, and no explicit transfer to -10 C is stated; moreover at -20 C the single-salt (blank) system retained far less capacity than the 0.5 M NaFSI double-salt (about 0 vs ~200 mAh at high rate), suggesting the baseline is weak but no -10 C measurement supports the target.

citations.quote: Ethylene carbonate (EC), propylene carbonate (PC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), methyl ethyl carbonate (EMC), dimethyl carbonate (DMC), $NaPF_{6}$ and NaFSI used in the electrolyte are all from the commercial products of Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co., Ltd. and not further purified. 3.1. Design and performance of the functional electrolyte
To begin with, in order to pre-evaluate the practicability of ether and carbonate ester as the electrolyte in pouch cells, comparative tests were first carried out, as shown in Fig. S1. Although the ether electrolytes have a high initial capacity, their cycling stability is poor, with a capacity retention rate of only 77.38 after 105 cycles, while the carbonate electrolytes have a capacity retention rate of 87.49 %. The gas production behaviour of ether and carbonate ester during long-term cycling at a cut-off voltage of 4.0 V at 45°C was monitored using differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (Fig. S2). It was observed that ether produced a greater quantity of gases, including methane and carbon monoxide, in comparison to carbonate ester. This may be a contributing factor to the unsuitability of ether for use in pouch cells, due to the rapid consumption of electrolyte, which results in a rapid decline in battery capacity. The electrolyte formula employs a combination of 1 mol/L NaPF $_{6}$ , cyclic ester EC and linear ester EMC in a mass ratio of 3:7 (called Baseline electrolyte), augmented by the incorporation of 3 wt% TMSS as a functional additive. The introduction of linear esters engenders a reduction in viscosity and an enhanced capacity to dissolve sodium salts in the electrolyte as a whole, thereby facilitating an improvement in the fluidity and ion conductivity of the electrolyte. Compounds containing sulfone groups, such as 1,3-propanesultone (PS), have been demonstrated to have excellent effects in inhibiting gas production and improving high-temperature performance (Fig. 1a). Consequently, they have been introduced into electrolytes and have become widely used. Compounds containing siloxane structures, such as trimethylsilyl isocyanate, exhibit high reactivity due to the facile rupture of their Si-O bonds. This enables effective removal of moisture and acid from the electrolyte and protection of the electrode electrolyte interface phase [25,26]. Therefore, the incorporation of TMSS is anticipated to combine the aforementioned effects with functional electrolytes, thereby achieving high-performance NFM/HC SIBs.

The potential function of TMSS in the electrolyte is also evaluated through DFT theoretical calculations. Fig. 1b lists the HOMO and LUMO energy levels of a series of molecul

citations.quote:
2.1. Preparation of the batteries
Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), ethylene carbonate (EC) and methyl ethyl carbonate (EMC) were supplied by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. NaPF $_6$ was dissolved into a EC and EMC (EC: EMC = 3:7 in wt.%) mixture to prepare baseline electrolyte (1 mol/L). Trimethylsilyl methanesulfonate additive (97 %, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was added into the baseline electrolyte to form functional electrolyte. NFM and HC active materials were purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. and Kuraray Co., Ltd., respectively. The NFM cathode was fabricated from NFM active material, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotubes (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P) and maleic acid dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) at a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated onto an aluminium substrate. The HC anode was contained 95 % HC, 1.5 % carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), 2.0 % styrene butadiene rubber (SBR), and 1.5 % super P. A Celgard 2700 membrane (Xingyuan Materials Co., Ltd) was as the separator. The mass loading of cathode and anode was 33.0 mg cm $^{-2}$ and 20.1 mg cm $^{-2}$ , respectively. The negative-to-positive (N/P) capacity ratio was 1.1. The empty pouch cells were dried under vacuum at 80 °C for 72 h, then transferred to a glove box and injected 6.0 g electrolyte. Other operations not mentioned were all carried out using the general methods in the battery manufacture.

citations.quote:
A B S T R A C T
A type of wide temperature range electrolyte design strategy incorporating trifunctional trimethylsilyl methanesulfonate (TMSS) additive in specific carbonate ester is developed to enhance the all-climate performance of commercial pouch $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). The incorporation of TMSS serves optimizing the solvation structure to accelerate the reaction kinetics, eliminating residual $H_{2}O/HF$ from the electrolyte, and promoting the formation of high-quality interface films. The capacity retention of the pouch NFM/HC cells with TMSS is effectively enhanced at high-voltage of 4.0 V and wide-temperature range from $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The cell delivers a high capacity retention of 80 % after 700 cycles at $25\ ^{\circ}C$ , while the initial energy density is as high as 117 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and maintains 103 Wh kg $^{-1}$ after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ and 1C (1C = 900 mA), achieving an 18.2 % increase in energy density. In addition, no obvious gas evolution can be observed when pouch cell is stored at $60\ ^{\circ}C$ and the low-temperature discharge at $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ achieves a 14.76 % increase in capacity at 0.5C. This work demonstrates the feasibility of TMSS in SIBs, and also put insight on the rational electrolyte design of SIBs.

It is well established that sodium-ion batteries exhibit superior low-temperature performance compared to lithium-ion batteries. This attribute is of significant potential value for their future applications $[32]$ . Due to the sluggish interfacial kinetics, the energy density and cycle life of SIBs suffer severely at subzero temperatures $[33]$ . Consequently, the electrochemical performance of electrolytes with and without TMSS was evaluated at extreme temperatures. Fig. 3c illustrates that the electrolyte containing TMSS exhibited superior cycling stability and capacity retention compared to the baseline electrolyte at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ with a 0.3C charge and 0.5C discharge. Batteries without TMSS exhibited a significant decline in capacity, retaining only 60% of their initial capacity after 40 cycles. This was attributed to their low coulombic efficiency and high polarization.

citations.quote:
A carbonate-based electrolyte containing a self-synthesized trimethylsilyl-benzenesulfonate (TMSBS) multifunctional additive is developed to enhance the all-climate performance of pouch $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) over a wide range from -30 to 60 °C. The pouch cells exhibit an 18.1% increase in capacity retention after 250 cycles at room temperature and an 11.3% increase after 240 cycles at 45 °C. The low-temperature discharging of different rates at -30 °C and the cycling at -10 °C demonstrate the adaptability of TMSBS-containing electrolytes at low temperatures. Compared to traditional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte can prevent excessive dissolution of interfacial films of two electrodes, purify undesirable substances of electrolyte composition, and optimize electrode interfaces and solvation structure. In addition, based on the gas analysis in the cyclic process at 45 °C and the storage at 60 °C by employing both in-situ and non-in-situ techniques, it reveals that TMSBS can suppress the side reactions of gas evolution, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs. This work presents a practical strategy for upgrading commercial SIBs and highlights the importance of rational electrolyte design for practical applications.

citations.quote: Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

citations.quote: The effect of sodium salts on the safety is also an important factor for commercial SIBs, and the corrosion of battery devices is one of the reference bases for sodium salt selection. Fig. 3e and f shows the corrosion results of Al foil in different electrolytes. As is reported at previous research, NaFSI-E would corrode Al foil during cycling so that may cause safety issues where NaDFOB-E and $\mathrm{NaPF_6 - E}$ hardly react. The coin cell was used to evaluate the corrosion of Al foil in different electrolytes. Surprisingly, although it can still observe obvious corrosion products on the glass fiber after cycling with NaFSI-E when measured with the coin cell, the Al foil inside the SIBs remains integrity, but the battery shell has obvious corrosion traces, as shown in Fig. 3g, which is quite different from the result measured by the electrolytic tank as shown in Fig. 3h. From this phenomenon, it can be inferred that NaFSI-E would corrode Al foil as well as stainless steel but corrode stainless steel first. Battery performance is the most straightly and convincing evidence to evaluate the electrolytes with different sodium salts. At present stage, NFM and HC are widely considered as ideal cathode and anode materials for commercial pouch SIBs due to their duration to water and air $[23–26]$ .

citations.quote: In this work, we have systemically evaluated and compared the discrepancy of SIBs applying different sodium salts from the view of the salt nature themselves, the properties of corresponding electrolytes, the battery performance and characterization analysis. Although $NaPF_{6}$ has been widely applied in SIBs, NaDFOB and NaFSI should also be paid more attention to broaden their application prospects in SIBs. Thereinto, owing to the limited solubility, single NaDFOB is not suitable for low temperature or high concentration electrolyte. The NaDFOB-E electrolyte enables the cells better performance than $NaPF_{6}-E$ , and is not corrosive to Al foil, indicating NaDFOB is a promising salt choice for room and high temperature electrolyte. Benefit to the superior viscosity, conductivity, and SEI/CEI, the low temperature performance of the cells with NaFSI-E is much better than that of other cells, and after solving the corrosion of NaFSI by additive, NaFSI-E is suitable for low temperature application.

reviews.reason: The candidate matches the studied NaPF6-E formulation and pouch NFM||HC format, and its Al-collector corrosion requirement is supported, but the central -10 °C low-temperature requirement is refuted (NaPF6-E cells suffer 'sudden death' after 50 cycles) and shell (stainless-steel) corrosion is only demonstrated for NaFSI-E, not NaPF6-E. The evidence therefore supports a held decision rather than recommending this candidate for the low-temperature, corrosion-free target.
reviews.association: The cited performance and corrosion observations come from the same Fan et al. study that prepared the exact NaPF6-E formulation (0.8 M NaPF6 in EC:EMC = 3:7) in NFM||HC pouch cells with Al-substrate electrodes in a plastic-laminated aluminum pouch, so the formulation, cell chemistry, and test platform correspond to the target. However, the Al-foil corrosion negative observation supports only the collector requirement, whereas the shell-corrosion finding is specific to NaFSI-E and was not duplicated for NaPF6-E. The -10 °C cycling result (Fig. 4g/h) is measured on these NaPF6-E pouch cells and is the direct low-temperature evidence.

2.1. Preparation of the functional electrolytes and batteries
Ethylene carbonate (EC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), $NaPF_{6}$ , NaFSI and NaDFOB were provided by the Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. NaFSI, $NaPF_{6}$ and NaDFOB ( $\geq98\%$ ) were also provided by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd (Table S1). Three electrolytes with 0.8 M concentration were all prepared by dissolving sodium salt in a mixture of EC: EMC = 3:7, and the electrolytes were represented as X-E, where X was the lithium salt used. All electrolytes were prepared in a dry argon filled glove box with both moisture and oxygen concentrations below 0.1 ppm. $NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_{2}$ (NFM) active material was purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co, Ltd, hard carbon (HC) active material was purchased from Kuraray Co Ltd. Pouch cells were assembled using a NFM cathode (120 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1C), a HC (290 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.05C) anode, and a celgard 2700 separator. For the preparation of NFM cathode, NFM, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotube (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and Maleic acid were dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) with a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate. For the HC anode, HC, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and conductive carbon black (Super P) with a mass ratio of 95:1.5:2:1.5 were mixed and dispersed in water, and then the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate. The areal loading of the anode and cathode was 16 g m $^{-2}$ and 33 g m $^{-2}$ , respectively. The cell cores were prepared by stacking with a separator separating the anodes (11) and cathodes (10), and then packaged in a plastic-laminated aluminum pouch. The resultant pouch cell was dried under vacuum at 80 °C for 72 h before being moved into a glove box for injecting electrolyte. The size of prepared pouch cells was 52 mm × 5 mm × 100 mm. All other preparations involved were carried out using methods commonly used in commercial battery manufacturing.

citations.quote: Based on the coupling of difluorophosphate-group with -tris(trimethylsilyl)-group of tris(trimethylsilyl)difluorophosphate (TDFP) additive and a “formation-repair” film-forming strategy, a difluorophosphate-based functional electrolyte is developed. This electrolyte facilitates the formation of tough and rich-NaF interfacial films on two electrodes and achieves an enhanced temperature performance of $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) over a wide range from $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . Compared to the cells without TDFP, the capacity retention of pouch NFM/HC cells with TDFP after 400 cycles at $25\ ^{\circ}C$ increases from 0% to 90%, stable cycling performance is obtained after 150 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ , and even the discharge capacity at $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ and the capacity retention after storage at $60\ ^{\circ}C$ are also greatly improved. In addition, the unique properties of TDFP differ from sodium difluorophosphate (NaDFP) and tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphate (TMSP) are analyzed to elucidate the functional mechanisms of TDFP. It is demonstrated that TDFP can not only catalyze the decomposition of $PF_{6}^{-}$ to form NaF-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI)/cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) films but also produce $PO_{2}F_{2}^{-}$ to optimize the film composition.

3.1. Design and performance of the functional electrolyte
To begin with, in order to pre-evaluate the practicability of ether and carbonate ester as the electrolyte in pouch cells, comparative tests were first carried out, as shown in Fig. S1. Although the ether electrolytes have a high initial capacity, their cycling stability is poor, with a capacity retention rate of only 77.38 after 105 cycles, while the carbonate electrolytes have a capacity retention rate of 87.49 %. The gas production behaviour of ether and carbonate ester during long-term cycling at a cut-off voltage of 4.0 V at 45°C was monitored using differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (Fig. S2). It was observed that ether produced a greater quantity of gases, including methane and carbon monoxide, in comparison to carbonate ester. This may be a contributing factor to the unsuitability of ether for use in pouch cells, due to the rapid consumption of electrolyte, which results in a rapid decline in battery capacity. The electrolyte formula employs a combination of 1 mol/L NaPF $_{6}$ , cyclic ester EC and linear ester EMC in a mass ratio of 3:7 (called Baseline electrolyte), augmented by the incorporation of 3 wt% TMSS as a functional additive. The introduction of linear esters engenders a reduction in viscosity and an enhanced capacity to dissolve sodium salts in the electrolyte as a whole, thereby facilitating an improvement in the fluidity and ion conductivity of the electrolyte. Compounds containing sulfone groups, such as 1,3-propanesultone (PS), have been demonstrated to have excellent effects in inhibiting gas production and improving high-temperature performance (Fig. 1a). Consequently, they have been introduced into electrolytes and have become widely used. Compounds containing siloxane structures, such as trimethylsilyl isocyanate, exhibit high reactivity due to the facile rupture of their Si-O bonds. This enables effective removal of moisture and acid from the electrolyte and protection of the electrode electrolyte interface phase [25,26]. Therefore, the incorporation of TMSS is anticipated to combine the aforementioned effects with functional electrolytes, thereby achieving high-performance NFM/HC SIBs.

citations.quote: A type of wide temperature range electrolyte design strategy incorporating trifunctional trimethylsilyl methanesulfonate (TMSS) additive in specific carbonate ester is developed to enhance the all-climate performance of commercial pouch $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). The incorporation of TMSS serves optimizing the solvation structure to accelerate the reaction kinetics, eliminating residual $H_{2}O/HF$ from the electrolyte, and promoting the formation of high-quality interface films. The capacity retention of the pouch NFM/HC cells with TMSS is effectively enhanced at high-voltage of 4.0 V and wide-temperature range from $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The cell delivers a high capacity retention of 80 % after 700 cycles at $25\ ^{\circ}C$ , while the initial energy density is as high as 117 Wh kg $^{-1}$ and maintains 103 Wh kg $^{-1}$ after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ and 1C (1C = 900 mA), achieving an 18.2 % increase in energy density. In addition, no obvious gas evolution can be observed when pouch cell is stored at $60\ ^{\circ}C$ and the low-temperature discharge at $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ achieves a 14.76 % increase in capacity at 0.5C. This work demonstrates the feasibility of TMSS in SIBs, and also put insight on the rational electrolyte design of SIBs.

During the charge and discharge process, TMSS is capable of capturing the HF generated by the hydrolysis of $PF_{6}^{-}$ in the solvent due to the presence of trace amounts of water. This protects the positive electrode material from corrosion and reduces the dissolution of transition metal ions. Additionally, the S = O group of the abundant charge carrier can stabilize $PF_{5}$ , reduce the opening of the solvent EC, and thus reduce the gas production of the pouch cells. This ensures that the battery will remain in good working order under conditions of high temperature. In order to choose the optimal concentration, part of the tough condition performance corresponding to different addition amounts of two additives is shown in Fig. S3. Considering cost and performance comprehensively, a 1:1.5 proportioning of NaDFP to TMSB or TMSB is chosen as the most suitable ratio. First, under the room and high temperatures, the emphasis of pouch cells with different electrolytes was given to the rate, cycling and storage performance parameters. The pouch cells with NB, NP, or NaDFP-containing electrolytes generally exhibit higher performance parameters than the cells with the baseline electrolyte. Under the room temperature of 25 °C, as shown in the Fig. S4a and S4b, rate and cycling performance of the pouch cells with the NB and NP-containing electrolytes is improved comparing to the cells with the baseline electrolyte, which can easily ascribed to the superior conductivity and lower desolvation energy. To further verify the effect of NP, NB, and NaDFP electrolytes at tougher conditions, rate, cycling, and storage tests at 45 °C and 60 °C were performed.

The main raw materials used for preparing functional electrolytes, including EC, EMC, $NaPF_{6}$ , NaDFP, TMSP and TMSB were provided by the Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. The baseline electrolyte was prepared by dissolving $NaPF_{6}$ in a mixture of EC: EMC=3:7 to form a concentration of 0.8 mol $L^{-1}$ . Then, NaDFP was added into the baseline electrolyte to prepare the NaDFP electrolyte, and NaDFP and

TMSB or TMSP were respectively added into the baseline electrolyte and assigned as NB or NP electrolyte. All electrolytes were prepared in a dry argon filled glove box with both moisture and oxygen concentrations below 0.1 ppm. NFM was purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co, Ltd, HC was purchased from Kuraray Co Ltd. The pouch test cells with NFM cathode (120 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1 C), HC anode (290 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.05 C), and Celgard 2700 separator were assembled using the conventional assembly method. Therein, NFM active material, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotube (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and Maleic acid (the reason of addition maleic acid was shown in Table 1) were dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) with a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate to prepare the NFM cathode.

citations.quote: With the help of "hard-soft synergy", polarization and capacity fading are alleviated signally during the cycling. Besides, rate performance of pouch cells is also improved by the synergistic effect of NP or NB electrolyte even at $-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1\mathrm{C}$ , as shown in Fig. 4d and S5b. Furthermore, to evaluate dual additive potential at tougher low-temperatures, $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ discharge tests are necessary. Fig. 4e shows the capacity retention of pouch cells at different discharge currents, revealing the cells all can exhibit good electrochemical performance under the tested temperature conditions. Even at $-30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1\mathrm{C}$ , the discharge capacity of pouch cells with NP and NB electrolytes still achieves $729\mathrm{mAh}$ and $697\mathrm{mAh}$ , respectively. These results confirm that this co-additive addition strategy improves extremely low temperature performance of NFM/HC pouch cells. Summarily, compared to single additive or baseline electrolyte, NFM/HC pouch cells with multi-component functional electrolyte possess much better performance. Therein, the cells containing NP electrolyte have better room and high-temperature performance, and the cells containing NB electrolyte are more suitable for low-temperature application.

citations.chunk_id: 0016_Fan 等 - 2025 - Electrolyte salts for large-scale application of sodium-ion batteries NaPF6 and emerging alternativ::sec3::child0
citations.quote: Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

citations.chunk_id: 0016_Fan 等 - 2025 - Electrolyte salts for large-scale application of sodium-ion batteries NaPF6 and emerging alternativ::sec8::child2
citations.quote: Besides, the physicochemical properties of three electrolytes containing NaDFOB (NaDFOB-E), $NaPF_{6}$ ( $NaPF_{6}-E$ ), and NaFSI (NaFSI-E) were measured. The solubility of three salts at different temperatures in the commonly used commercial solvent combinations (EC/EMC = 1:1) was tested. It was indicated that the solubility of NaDFOB was significantly lower than that of the other two salts, as shown in Fig. 1c and Fig. S1, indicating NaDFOB might not be suitable for high concentration or low temperature electrolyte as a main salt. Thus, the 0.8 M electrolytes containing different sodium salts were further investigated. The LSV curves of the electrolytes in the voltage range of 2.0–5.5 V (vs. Na/Na $^{+}$ ) were used to evaluate the electrochemical stable window (ESW) of electrolytes. As shown in Fig. 1d, no obvious oxidation current peaks were observed in NaPF $_{6}$ -E and NaDFOB-E below 4.5 V. The oxidation current peak of NaFSI-E increased far more sharply when the voltage exceeded 4.0 V, which might be attributed to the instability of FSI $^{-}$ anions under higher voltage. The density of three electrolytes (0.8 M) is shown in Fig. 1e, where injection amount of NaFSI-E might much more than other. In addition, the viscosity and conductivity are also important properties for commercial electrolyte, which deeply affects the performance of SIBs, especially at the low temperature.

citations.quote:
3.2. Performance of the batteries with different electrolytes
The effect of sodium salts on the safety is also an important factor for commercial SIBs, and the corrosion of battery devices is one of the reference bases for sodium salt selection. Fig. 3e and f shows the corrosion results of Al foil in different electrolytes. As is reported at previous research, NaFSI-E would corrode Al foil during cycling so that may cause safety issues where NaDFOB-E and $\mathrm{NaPF_6 - E}$ hardly react. The coin cell was used to evaluate the corrosion of Al foil in different electrolytes. Surprisingly, although it can still observe obvious corrosion products on the glass fiber after cycling with NaFSI-E when measured with the coin cell, the Al foil inside the SIBs remains integrity, but the battery shell has obvious corrosion traces, as shown in Fig. 3g, which is quite different from the result measured by the electrolytic tank as shown in Fig. 3h. From this phenomenon, it can be inferred that NaFSI-E would corrode Al foil as well as stainless steel but corrode stainless steel first.

Battery performance is the most straightly and convincing evidence to evaluate the electrolytes with different sodium salts. At present stage, NFM and HC are widely considered as ideal cathode and anode materials for commercial pouch SIBs due to their duration to water and air $[23–26]$ . The electrochemical performance of NFM||HC pouch SIBs with various electrolytes including $NaPF_{6}$ , NaFSI and NaDFOB from $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ to $70\ ^{\circ}C$ , have been thoroughly investigated. The rate capability of the cells with different electrolytes at various current densities under $45\ ^{\circ}C$ was firstly studied, as illustrated in Fig. 4a. The $NaPF_{6}-E$ and NaFSI-E cells showed similar rate capabilities, while the NaDFOB-E cell exhibited inferior performance. Conversely, the cycling performance as shown in Fig. 4b indicated that the NaDFOB-E and NaFSI-E cells were more stable than the $NaPF_{6}-E$ cell, and following $70\ ^{\circ}C$ storage experiment results also confirmed that NaDFOB-E and NaFSI-E cells had better performance than $NaPF_{6}-E$ cell, as shown in Fig. 4c.

citations.chunk_id: 0045_Lu 等 - 2025 - All-climate carbonate electrolyte with 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride additive leads the way to high-perfo::sec2::child0
citations.quote: A multifunctional additive, 2-sulfobenzoic anhydride (SA), was synthesized from the readily available saccharin, then 1 % SA was added into carbonate-based electrolytes to enhance the performance of pouch sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) employing $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM) cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes across a wide temperature range from $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ . The commercial pouch cells delivered a capacity retention of 90.52 % after 300 cycles at room temperature and 92.28 % after 300 cycles at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ . Low-temperature rate performance at $-20\ ^{\circ}C$ and cycling at $-10\ ^{\circ}C$ further demonstrated the excellent adaptability of SA-containing electrolytes under sub-zero temperature. Moreover, under high-voltage operation at 4.0 V, the SA-containing electrolyte effectively suppressed capacity fading, resulting in an 11.44 % improvement in capacity retention. Compared to conventional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte enables interfacial optimization by suppressing excessive growth of cathode and anode interphases, also it eliminates detrimental electrolyte components, tune the solvation structure and promote interfacial reaction kinetics. In situ gas analysis conducted during cycling at $45\ ^{\circ}C$ revealed that SA significantly inhibits gas-evolving side reactions, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs.

In summary, we have successfully synthesized a multifunctional SA electrolyte additive for pouch NFM/HC sodium-ion batteries, enabling stable electrochemical performance across a wide operating temperature range ( $-20$ to $60\ ^{\circ}C$ ). The multifunctional role of the SA-containing electrolyte can be attributed to a combination of synergistic effects, including the regulation of $Na^{+}$ solvation structure to accelerate interfacial reaction kinetics and enhance electrochemical stability at low temperatures, the scavenging residual water to preserve the structural stability of the cathode and suppress excessive gas evolution, thereby enhancing high-temperature performance, and the preferential redox decomposition of SA on the anode surface to form a high-quality interfacial film that protects the electrode and reduces interfacial resistance. Collectively, this work provides new insights into the rational design and optimization of electrolyte additives for practical all-climate pouch SIBs and other advanced energy storage systems.

citations.quote: Under more extreme conditions, discharge tests at $-20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 4a) revealed that cells with SA-based electrolyte delivered discharge capacities of 758.6, 702.2 and $638.2\mathrm{mAh}$ at $0.2\mathrm{C}$ , $0.5\mathrm{C}$ , and $1\mathrm{C}$ ( $1\mathrm{C} = 900\mathrm{mA}$ ), respectively, outperforming those with the baseline electrolyte, which exhibited 706.3, 636.8 and $563.6\mathrm{mAh}$ . These results confirm that SA facilitates higher energy density and improved capacity retention at low temperatures, rendering it well-suited for emergency storage applications in cold environments. In addition, the rate capability of sodium-ion batteries at ambient temperature is critical for practical deployment. High-rate performance enables rapid charge/discharge cycles, a requirement for power-intensive applications such as electric vehicles and portable electronics [27a,28]. As shown in Fig. 4d, the SA containing system exhibited superior rate capacity, indicating enhanced commercial viability. Long-term cycling at 1C was also evaluated at room temperature (Figs. 4c and S7). During extended cycling, the baseline electrolyte showed faster polarization growth, whereas the SA-based system demonstrated superior capacity retention and enhanced coulombic efficiency. These characteristics contribute to reduced energy losses and extended battery lifespan, which are advantageous for grid-scale and commercial energy storage [29].

4. Conclusions
In summary, we have successfully synthesized a multifunctional TMSBS additive for the advanced electrolyte of pouch NFM/HC cells, achieving exceptional performance across an extended operational temperature range ( $-30-60\ ^{\circ}C$ ). The multifunctional mechanism of TMSBS-containing electrolytes can be elucidated through three synergistic pathways: (i) optimization of the solvation structure to promote faster reaction kinetics, achieve better performance at low temperatures, and elevate the electrochemical stability window of the electrolyte; (ii) preferential oxidation-reduction decomposition on the anode surface to form a high-quality interfacial film to protect the electrode and reduce the impedance of the battery; (iii) capture of HF and moisture, ensuring the structural stability of the cathode material and suppressing the production of excess gas to improve high-temperature performance. Therefore, this study provides new ideas for the design and optimization of electrolyte additives for commercial all-climate pouch SIBs and other energy storage devices.

A B S T R A C T
A carbonate-based electrolyte containing a self-synthesized trimethylsilyl-benzenesulfonate (TMSBS) multifunctional additive is developed to enhance the all-climate performance of pouch $NaNi_{0.33}Fe_{0.33}Mn_{0.33}O_{2}$ (NFM)/hard carbon (HC) sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) over a wide range from -30 to 60 °C. The pouch cells exhibit an 18.1% increase in capacity retention after 250 cycles at room temperature and an 11.3% increase after 240 cycles at 45 °C. The low-temperature discharging of different rates at -30 °C and the cycling at -10 °C demonstrate the adaptability of TMSBS-containing electrolytes at low temperatures. Compared to traditional commercial electrolytes, this electrolyte can prevent excessive dissolution of interfacial films of two electrodes, purify undesirable substances of electrolyte composition, and optimize electrode interfaces and solvation structure. In addition, based on the gas analysis in the cyclic process at 45 °C and the storage at 60 °C by employing both in-situ and non-in-situ techniques, it reveals that TMSBS can suppress the side reactions of gas evolution, thereby ensuring the safety of SIBs. This work presents a practical strategy for upgrading commercial SIBs and highlights the importance of rational electrolyte design for practical applications.

2.1. Preparation of the batteries
Sodium hexafluorophosphate (NaPF $_6$ ), ethylene carbonate (EC), and methyl ethyl carbonate (EMC) were supplied by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. NaPF $_6$ was dissolved into a mixture of EC and EMC (EC: EMC = 3:7 in wt%) to prepare Baseline electrolyte (1 mol L $^{-1}$ ). TMSBS additive (1 wt%) was added to the Baseline electrolyte to form a functional electrolyte. NFM and HC active materials were purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. and Kuraray Co., Ltd., respectively. The NFM cathode was fabricated from NFM active material, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotubes (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and maleic acid dispersed in $N$ -methylpyrrolidone (NMP) at a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated onto an aluminium substrate. The HC anode contained 95% HC, 1.5% carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), 2.0% styrene butadiene rubber (SBR), and 1.5% Super P. A Celgard 2700 membrane (Xingyuan Materials Co., Ltd) was used as the separator. The mass loading of the cathode and anode was 33.0 and 20.1 mg cm $^{-2}$ , respectively. The negative-to-positive (N/P) capacity ratio was 1.1. The empty pouch cells were dried under vacuum at 80 °C for 72 h, then transferred to a glove box, and injected 6.0 g of electrolyte. Other operations not mentioned were all carried out using the general methods in the battery manufacture.
